llms-how-they-work.context_blurb:
Every chatbot people actually use runs on the same kind of program, and Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT are all large language models that predict text. The name is Large Language Model, shortened to LLM, and the large refers to the model's size in parameters and training data. Hold on to one picture of what it is doing and most chatbot news becomes readable.

The mechanism fits in a sentence. The model predicts the most likely next piece of text given everything before it, then the next, then the next, and that loop is the whole trick. That is why the answer streams onto the screen in pieces: each token is chosen based on the text so far, not a fixed answer the model committed to at the start. It also explains why the same question twice gives different replies, because the model samples from a probability distribution over possible next tokens, so high-probability words can each be chosen on different runs.

What makes it large is scale in two directions, since the model has a huge number of internal numbers, called parameters, and is trained on a huge amount of text. The training text runs to trillions of words drawn from books, websites, code, and other sources. GPT-3 had around 175 billion parameters, far larger than predecessors at the time. Imagine one glass marble per parameter: you would fill swimming pools, not a teacup, and the count is past picturing.

Fluency is not thought. When a chatbot writes that it thinks the sky is blue, it is producing words it learned from training, with nothing behind them. When its answer looks like careful working, it is generating words that LOOK like reasoning by predicting what reasoning text usually sounds like. In 2021 a paper by Emily Bender with Timnit Gebru and others nicknamed these systems stochastic parrots, and the label earns its keep because it captures the core mechanic of repeating statistical patterns from training data, without claiming the model understands what it says.

Four limits follow directly from the mechanism. First, a plain model cannot really answer with live data, since its training stopped months before today. Its words come from patterns learned during training, not from a search run on your behalf, so for this morning's events use a search engine like Google, because chatbots often don't know recent events at all. Second, predicting text is not computing, so it predicts a number that looks plausible from training text, instead of running the actual multiplication algorithm. Multiplying two big numbers is the task it handles worst, and multi-step arithmetic by hand without a calculator tool is where it falls over. Check the result with a real calculator, or reach for a calculator app in the first place. Third, memory: by default each new chat starts fresh from blank. Fourth, and worst, they can be confidently wrong, and the smooth voice is no clue at all.

So match the tool to the job: chatbot for drafting, search for the weather. Live schedules and prices belong to a flight search website. The general rule is chatbot for explanation and drafting, search engine for current facts and primary sources. Among the common uses, the two wrong ones are arithmetic and current news, because pattern-completion isn't computation and a vanilla LLM has no live web access. Underneath sits a difference in kind: a search engine finds existing web pages while an LLM produces new text by predicting tokens, which may match nothing that exists. Search returns where the information came from, while an LLM returns text whose source you cannot inspect, so who said this is a question only search can answer.

Three last pieces. The wording you type matters enough to have a name, prompt engineering, because the same model answers a vague question and a precise one quite differently. A Google paper in 2022 found that asking a model to think step by step lifted accuracy on school maths from about eighteen percent to near eighty, a technique called chain-of-thought prompting, where the user asks the model to write out its reasoning before giving a final answer. And when a support window answers you in seconds with no employee involved, that is a chatbot AI. In fiction, fans of Kubrick's 2001 noticed that the three letters of HAL sit one position back from IBM in the alphabet, a reading the film's co-writer later denied, saying the name stood instead for a heuristically programmed algorithmic computer.

transformers-and-attention.context_blurb: Modern AI chatbots are built on a particular design of neural network that overtook the field in the late 2010s. Every major chatbot you have heard of uses it underneath. The design's defining trick is that it lets the model consider many words of the conversation at the same time, in parallel, instead of reading one word after another the way older AI language systems worked. That change made it practical to train on huge datasets using the kind of hardware ordinarily built for video-game graphics, which is why the current AI boom is so tied to specialized chip supplies. This family of architectures is the quiet engine behind almost everything in the current AI era — chatbots, coding tools, image models, multimodal systems. Media coverage from this decade onward will keep assuming you know what this family is called, so recognizing the name on sight is worth more than any one technical detail about how it works. Several researchers at a large US tech company introduced the design in a single academic paper, which the field now treats as foundational — a surprising amount of modern AI history traces back to a handful of such papers, and this one is near the top.

tokens-and-context-window.context_blurb: When you talk to a chatbot the model does not actually read whole words the way you do. It chops your text into small pieces and processes those. That chopping scheme is why models sometimes spell words strangely or miscount letters — the model is not working at the letter level. The second idea that goes with those pieces is a fixed limit on how much of the current conversation the model can still see at once. Modern chatbots have large but finite limits here. When a chat gets long enough, the oldest parts fall out of the window and the model loses track of them — names you established, decisions you made, facts you set up. The two concepts together explain a lot of odd chatbot behavior: why models sometimes spell strangely, why very long chats start to drift or forget what you said, why pasted documents have size limits, and why models tend to pay less attention to information buried in the middle of a very long prompt. In practice, a chatbot's 'memory' in a long conversation is a budget rather than a filing cabinet — once the budget overflows, the earliest content is gone unless the chat product has been designed to save notes between sessions, which is a separate feature bolted on top.

neural-networks-and-deep-learning.context_blurb: A neural network is the engine under almost every modern AI system. The name comes from a loose mid-twentieth-century analogy to brain cells, but the thing itself is pure math: layers of simple arithmetic units stacked between the input and the output, with huge numbers of adjustable settings inside that get tuned during training. The 'deep' in deep learning just means many layers. For most of AI's history this family of techniques was unpopular; it took off only once computers and datasets got large enough for it to work. The three researchers most associated with keeping the approach alive during the lean decades were later awarded the field's top computing prize together — one of the clearest cases in modern science of long-unfashionable research paying off. This is the common machinery behind image recognition, chatbots, voice assistants, and self-driving perception — one family of methods applied across many places that used to look like unrelated problems. Recognizing the family name and the fact that it is not literal 'brain modelling' (it is math inspired by a very loose analogy) is useful literacy, because popular writing often slides from the metaphor into claims the technology does not actually make.

training-pretraining-inference.context_blurb: An AI chatbot gets built in two very different stages. The first is long, slow, enormously expensive: the model studies piles of text and adjusts its many internal numbers. This happens once (or a few times) per model, often costing enormous amounts of money, running on huge clusters of specialized chips, consuming lots of electricity. The second stage is much cheaper and faster: using the trained model to answer each question, one chat reply at a time. The split matters because almost every important AI business and policy question — chip supply, data use, model releases, running AI on your own computer, export controls, environmental impact — ties back to the distinction between the one-time stage and the many-times stage. The useful thing to notice is that once a model has been through the first stage, the resulting file of trained numbers can in principle be copied, shipped, or run anywhere compatible hardware exists; the company that made it can control access only if it keeps the file to itself. That single property divides the AI industry into its two big camps — labs that ship only through controlled interfaces and labs that release the trained file publicly.

fine-tuning-and-rlhf.context_blurb:
A freshly trained language model is not an assistant. It is a completion engine that will carry on whatever text it is shown, helpful or vile, so every chatbot you have used went through a second stage of training on top. That stage is where the manners, the refusals and the politics come from.

The cheap version is fine-tuning, which means taking a pre-trained model and training it further on a narrow dataset: feed a general model nothing but recipes and you get a cooking helper. The reason nobody starts from scratch is money, because pre-training is enormously expensive, so fine-tuning piggybacks on that work and reshapes the model for a specific task cheaply. Split the job that way and the expensive pretraining is done once, and many specialized models can be cheaply fine-tuned from the same base. Stanford's Alpaca made the point unforgettable in 2023 for about six hundred dollars, because Meta's Llama had already learned grammar, common-sense reasoning, and world facts during its massive pretraining, so Alpaca only had to teach it the chatbot-reply style on top. The stage that teaches that style has its own name, instruction tuning, where the model is shown many examples of helpful responses to user requests.

Then comes the step that made chatbots feel like chatbots: RLHF, which stands for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. What the humans in the loop actually do is modest, because they rank candidate responses from best to worst, and the model learns to produce outputs that rank higher. Because people cannot rank millions of answers, their judgements train a reward model, which scores the main model's outputs at scale once it has learned from human ratings. The effect on the product is the whole reason it is done, since it makes the model behave like a helpful assistant instead of a raw text-predictor that completes anything.

Now the costs, which are the part worth remembering. Ranking is not truth-checking: raters can be misled by confident-sounding wrong answers, so RLHF can reward output that sounds right rather than is right. Nor is the process value-free, because whatever the raters happen to value gets baked into the model, including any political or cultural biases they bring. Put as a general warning, it can encode the rater pool's values into the model in ways that aren't obvious from the outside. Every run embeds decisions about which raters were hired, what rating instructions they were given, which responses were promoted, and which were demoted, so every step reflects somebody's values. Critics of the big labs press one version of this hard: if trainers, raters, and policy writers share political assumptions, those assumptions can quietly become product defaults. David Rozado's measurements of chatbot answers on standard political questionnaires are the evidence usually cited, and Google's 2024 image-generator fiasco is the visible case.

Safety training has a characteristic failure too. It can overshoot, refusing benign requests because they vaguely resemble unsafe ones, which is why a child's villain speech or a security researcher's question gets turned away. The drift has a name: overcorrection, or refusal creep, where alignment training tuned to avoid one set of failures starts producing a broader set of unhelpful refusals.

One last thing the marketing leaves out. The politeness was built by people, many of them contractors in Kenya and the Philippines, and reporters found that workers viewed traumatic content for low pay, with limited mental-health support and tight time pressure. Time magazine reported in January 2023 that Kenyan labellers working through the firm Sama were paid under two dollars an hour to tag violence and abuse so the model could learn to refuse it.

hallucination.context_blurb:
The industry's word for the central failure of chatbots is hallucination, which means the model produced confident-sounding text that turns out to be false or invented, with no real basis. It is not a bug awaiting a patch. It follows from how the thing works.

The mechanism explains everything else. A model answers by predicting likely next words from training patterns, with no separate machinery to check that what it produced refers to anything real. That is also why it never sounds unsure, because the model has no internal accuracy signal on a given topic, so there's nothing inside to express uncertainty. The doubt has to come from you.

The failures cluster, which is the practical gift. They land on specific dates, names, numbers, quotes and citations, exactly the things that need to be looked up. Two reasons stack up. Specific facts are sparse signals in training data, since many similar plausible alternatives exist, while broad descriptions have many redundant sources. And they are short, specific tokens, so any plausible-looking combination satisfies the model's surface goal of generating fluent text. By contrast, the safest ground is definitions and explanations of well-established ideas, where the training data repeats itself a thousand times.

So the habits are cheap and specific. For a quotation, search the exact quote in quotation marks to see if any real source has it, and do that before it goes in an essay. For a study, search for it to confirm it exists. For a link, click the URL before quoting; if it doesn't load, the source doesn't exist or the URL was fabricated. Fabricated links are common because URLs have a learnable structure, so the model produces plausible-looking strings that don't actually exist. For a number, remember that an LLM is excellent at producing precise-sounding numbers without any underlying source, because confidence isn't accuracy. Worse, specific numbers feel authoritative, so readers trust them more, and inventing them takes no extra model effort. And never ask a plain chatbot about tonight: with no live web access, the model produced a plausible-sounding time based on training-text patterns about football schedules, and that guess is almost certainly wrong.

Institutions get caught by the same thing, which is where the law has begun to speak. A passenger asked the chatbot on Air Canada's site what discount applied after a death in the family. The bot invented a refund policy the airline did not have, and when he claimed it the company argued it was not responsible for what the bot had said. In February 2024 a Canadian tribunal disagreed, so Air Canada was held liable, and companies are responsible for what their chatbots tell customers. The engineering answer that follows is constraint rather than cleverness: restrict the AI to known-good answers from approved content, and reject open-ended generation. For a student on the other side of such a bot, the habit is to check with a human at the school, because the AI may have made up the policy.

One last case shows the failure outside text. Whisper, OpenAI's speech-to-text model, is accurate overall, yet researchers found in 2024 that it sometimes invented sentences entirely, hallucinated text the speaker never said, which is dangerous in medical transcription. A tool that is usually accurate is fine for a podcast and risky in a hospital, and that is the same tool in both places. Several health systems had already put Whisper-based transcription into consulting rooms before the finding was published.

Two small calibrations finish the picture. The broad shape of an answer is usually sound while the fine detail is where the invention hides, so a paragraph about what photosynthesis does can be trusted further than the date beside a physicist's name in the same paragraph. And the tone tells you nothing at all, because an invented court case arrives in the same unhurried, polished prose as a real one, with no hedge and no warning.

embeddings-and-vector-search.context_blurb:
Embeddings are the trick that turns meaning into geometry, and they quietly run most of what consumer AI calls understanding your query. The idea is to represent a word, a sentence or a whole document as one very long row of numbers, a thousand of them in some systems, which places it as a point in a vast space.

Why bother with numbers? Because numbers let the model measure how similar two words are, by checking how close their lists are in space. King sits near queen; king sits nowhere near rutabaga. That geometry is the engine behind modern search, since similar meanings produce nearby numerical positions, so finding documents like this one becomes a geometric search rather than a keyword match. And it fixes the oldest weakness of keyword matching, because two texts can mean nearly the same thing without sharing any words, and embeddings catch the meaning overlap anyway. Ask how to stop a dog barking and you will be shown a guide to training a quiet puppy.

The famous demonstration came from Google researchers in 2013, with a model called word2vec. Take the numbers for king, subtract man, add woman, and you land beside queen, which reveals that concepts like gender and royalty live as directions in the number-space, so adding and subtracting them shifts meaning predictably.

One caution keeps the picture honest. No engineer sets those numbers by hand and no reader can interpret them one at a time, because they are different features the model has learned to track, with no single number mapping cleanly to a human-readable concept. There is no slot for plural and no slot for verb. The structure lives in the relationships between points, not inside any one of them, which is why interpreting what a model has learned is a research field of its own.

scaling-laws-and-model-size.context_blurb: A striking finding of the modern AI era is that bigger tends to work better in a predictable way. If you make the model's parameter count larger, use more training data, and run more compute, the resulting model gets reliably better at predicting text — the gain follows a smooth mathematical curve rather than jumping around. Labs use these predictions to decide, before spending huge sums on a training run, roughly what a bigger model is likely to do. The scaling story is why frontier training runs now cost many hundreds of millions of dollars, why chip orders can swing national trade balances, and why the AI industry is remaking the geography of data centers and electricity. At some scale, qualitative new abilities emerged that smaller models did not show — the ability to pick up a new task from a few examples in the prompt, for one. This is contested territory: there are signs the easiest gains from pure scale may be slowing as the simplest 'make it bigger' approach runs into limits of available high-quality data and electricity. Nobody is certain how far it goes, and the scaling-vs-architecture argument is one of the field's live debates.

mixture-of-experts.context_blurb:
Mixture of Experts, written MoE, is the trick behind the odd figures in modern model announcements, where a laboratory boasts of hundreds of billions of parameters and the thing still runs fast and cheap.

The design splits the network into many parallel sub-networks, each called an expert, with a small router that reads each incoming piece of text and wakes only two or three of them while the rest stay idle. Engineers choose it over one giant dense network because it lets the model have a huge total parameter count while keeping the per-token computation cost much lower. Put as the economics, it lets a model store more knowledge total while spending less compute per query, since only the experts relevant to each input get activated.

The consequence for cost is worth stating precisely. GPT-4 has never been officially measured in public, but credible estimates describe a mixture-of-experts model with something like a trillion parameters in total and a couple of hundred billion firing for any one token. The gap matters because only the active parameters affect the cost of generating each token, even though all parameters must be stored. You pay memory for the whole model and arithmetic for the slice.

Two cautions. The word expert is loose, because these sub-networks are not interpretable specialists in chemistry or French; they are simply the paths the router learned to favour. And a huge mixture-of-experts model is harder to run at home than a dense model of the same speed, because the whole file still has to fit on your machine, which complicates the easy claim that open weights put frontier capability in everybody's hands.

multimodal-ai.context_blurb: A multimodal AI model is one that handles more than one kind of input in the same system — text plus images, sometimes also audio and video. Earlier chatbots only read text. A modern multimodal chatbot can take a photo you upload and discuss it, listen to a voice note, or watch a short video. The trick underneath is that every kind of input gets converted into the same sort of numerical representation and fed through the same core network — images get sliced into small patches that are treated almost like text tokens, audio gets turned into similar numerical pieces, and the model learns to work across all of them at once. This is why the current flagship chatbots can describe pictures, transcribe speech, help with code snippets, and discuss documents interchangeably. Recognizing the label will matter more and more as AI products get built around voice, cameras, and video rather than only typed text. It also matters for safety: once a model can read images, instructions hidden in images (image prompt injection) become a possible attack path that pure-text models did not have.

open-weight-vs-closed-api.context_blurb: Modern AI models come in two shapes that look similar from the outside but are structurally very different. Some only run on their company's servers; you talk to them through a controlled interface, and your conversation goes to the company. Others release the trained numbers as a downloadable file, so anyone with the right hardware can run them locally, modify them, or build on them. This distinction drives a long list of policy fights — about safety, privacy, competition, export controls, chip export rules, and who ends up in charge of frontier AI. The debate splits along real tradeoffs: closed models let a lab control misuse by filtering requests and refusing certain actions, while open models prevent a small group of companies from being the only ones who can run the technology. Once a capable model is released openly, it cannot be recalled — the file exists on thousands of hard drives and shows up on peer-to-peer networks. Safety training applied to the weights can be removed with modest fine-tuning. These are structural trade-offs, not rhetorical ones, and recognizing them is more useful than picking a side.

chatgpt-and-openai.context_blurb:
If you learn one AI company, learn this one. OpenAI built the product that dragged this technology out of the research journals and into every classroom, and nearly every argument since, about money, safety, copyright and governance, runs through it.

First the category. Software that sorts things into boxes, spam or not spam, cat or dog, is a discriminative model; ChatGPT and Stable Diffusion are generative, because they produce new content, whether words, images, or audio, that did not exist before. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok are all chatbot assistants, programs you talk to in plain language and get written answers back from. Those four names, from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI, are the real ones; a confident-sounding chatbot name that no such company has ever shipped is probably invented, so look it up. Under the hood each one is a chatbot running on a large language model, which generates text a token at a time rather than looking anything up.

OpenAI, the San Francisco lab that built ChatGPT, began in December 2015 as a non-profit AI research lab with a mission to build safe AGI that benefits everyone. Training frontier models turned out to cost billions, so in 2019 it created a capped-profit subsidiary, OpenAI LP, to raise large amounts of investment. That matters years later because the original mission, that AI benefits should be broadly shared, was a public promise, and the capped-profit shift signals whose interests are being served now. It also leaves a question nobody has answered: whether nonprofit governance can constrain the strategy of a capped-profit subsidiary that has its own commercial pressures and investor expectations. A 2018 charter clause promising to stand aside and help if a rival safety-minded project got there first has the same weakness, since it has no enforcement mechanism, only OpenAI itself decides whether another project qualifies, and nothing forces the company to stop or assist.

The models came in steps. In February 2019 the lab announced GPT-2 but released only a smaller version at first, citing the risk of mass-produced fake text. GPT-3 followed in 2020 with 175 billion parameters and a surprise nobody had predicted, few-shot learning: put two or three worked examples into the prompt and it does the task with no further training. It reached the public only through a programming interface, yet developers built early products on top of GPT-3, among them Jasper, Copy.ai, and Codex, proving demand and pointing to a chat-ready future. The last ingredient was manners. OpenAI added instruction tuning and RLHF, fine-tuning the model to follow user instructions and having humans rate its answers for quality. Credit where it belongs, though: Google invented the architecture, the transformer, in 2017, and OpenAI was the company that scaled it up into ChatGPT and brought it mainstream.

The launch itself was almost casual. ChatGPT appeared on November 30, 2022, released as a research preview with free public access. Two months later it had a hundred million users, the fastest of any consumer product on record, against about nine months for TikTok and two and a half years for Instagram. The reason was structural rather than magical: the product was free, low-friction, and immediately useful for a huge range of tasks, so adoption faced few barriers. What followed was the 2023 AI summer, when mainstream public attention crashed into AI for the first time, with Google declaring an internal emergency and every rival shipping a chatbot.

Two footnotes finish the arc. GPT-4, in March 2023, brought multimodality, meaning it could accept images as input and discuss them, not just text. Its exam scores made the headlines, and the careful objection was sound, because test-taking measures one slice of human capability, so passing one doesn't mean the model matches humans across other tasks. The same release broke with the lab's older habits: OpenAI was founded with a research-sharing mission and many researchers saw the shift to secrecy, a technical report that withheld the architecture, the training data and the size of the model, as a departure from it. And if your answers differ from a friend's, check which model you are on, since paid plans usually offer the newer or bigger model and the free plan a smaller or older one. That is exactly what ChatGPT Plus sold from the start at twenty dollars a month: priority access during high-traffic times and access to newer models before they reached the free tier.

claude-and-anthropic.context_blurb:
Anthropic is one of the handful of laboratories at the AI frontier, and its origin story is a disagreement. In 2021 a group of senior researchers walked out of OpenAI and set up a rival in San Francisco, saying that safety work needed independence from commercial product pressure.

The lab the Amodei team left to start Anthropic was OpenAI. Dario Amodei, an Italian-American researcher who had run OpenAI's research and shaped much of the GPT work, became chief executive of Anthropic, the lab that produces the Claude family of language models. The president is his sister, Daniela Amodei. Others came with them, among them Tom Brown, lead author of the GPT-3 paper, and Jared Kaplan. So the plain description is this: Anthropic is a US AI lab founded by former OpenAI researchers, now competing with its parent at the frontier. Its chatbot is called Claude, a nod to Claude Shannon, the mathematician who founded information theory in 1948. Anthropic built the Claude family of chatbots and pioneered Constitutional AI as a training technique.

That technique is where the safety claim becomes something you can inspect. Claude has been trained with a process called Constitutional AI that explicitly lists principles it should follow, among them helpfulness, honesty and harmlessness. The pipeline is odd and simple: the model answers, then criticises its own answer against the written rules, then rewrites it, and the revised answers become training data. Compared with paying human raters to score everything, the technique scales better without requiring human raters for every example, while encoding behavior preferences explicitly. Whether that is the right approach is contested; what matters is noticing that different laboratories make different choices, and that this one wrote its choices down.

Two structural details are worth the same scepticism you would bring to any company's self-description. Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation, a for-profit form that carries a stated social purpose in its charter, and the checking of that purpose falls largely to the company itself, since a PBC has no government inspector ensuring delivery. Patagonia uses the same form. It can be genuine and it can be marketing, and the way to tell is to read the charter and the incentives rather than the label. The sibling leadership is the other oddity, because a brother in charge with a sister as president places trust and personal alignment at the center of decision-making, a deliberate counter to lab dynamics shaped by external boards. The OpenAI board crisis of November 2023 showed what that failure mode looks like.

Why does a founding quarrel deserve a card of its own? Because it signaled that internal disagreements over safety-versus-speed at frontier AI labs were significant enough to drive whole teams to start a parallel company. Industry structure is evidence. When researchers leave to build a rival and say why, the explanation is worth reading closely, since it is their account of what they thought was wrong where they came from.

gemini-and-google-deepmind.context_blurb:
Google has been at this longer than almost anyone, which makes its slow start in chatbots the strangest story in the industry. Its researchers invented the architecture every modern chatbot runs on, and its London laboratory produced the era's biggest scientific results, and still a smaller rival reached the public first.

The laboratory is DeepMind, based in London, founded there in 2010 by Demis Hassabis with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman. By 2013 it had programs learning old Atari games from the pixels alone, and in 2014 it was bought by Google, which has run DeepMind as a research lab inside Alphabet ever since, for a price around half a billion dollars. The deal carried a condition unusual for a technology buyout, an independent ethics board that would oversee DeepMind's AI research separately from Google management, though its membership and powers were never made public. In 2023 Google merged DeepMind with its other big laboratory, Google Brain, under Hassabis.

Google Brain is where another figure in this story sat. Andrew Ng co-founded it, and he had already taught a free Stanford machine-learning class to more than a hundred thousand students, which led him to start an online-course company in 2012: Coursera, founded with Daphne Koller, also a Stanford computer-science professor. A generation of practitioners learned the subject from that course.

The consumer product took longer and changed names. Google launched a chatbot in March 2023 called Bard, which stumbled in its demonstrations and never caught on. In February 2024 the company rebranded it and folded it into search, and the Google entry in the chatbot line-up beside ChatGPT, Claude and Grok is Gemini. Its advantage is reach rather than persuasion, since it appears inside search results, Android phones and the office apps people already use. That reach cuts both ways, as the image-generation fiasco of the same month demonstrated to the whole world at once.

xai-and-grok.context_blurb: Elon Musk was one of OpenAI's early funders before leaving its board in the late 2010s. After ChatGPT's success he publicly complained about OpenAI's direction, filed lawsuits over its shift away from the original non-profit mission, and launched a new AI lab of his own. Its chatbot is deeply integrated with the social-media platform Musk also owns, giving it real-time access to the platform's posts and a different content-moderation posture from the mainstream US chatbots. The chatbot's name is borrowed from a mid-twentieth-century science-fiction novel. Recognizing this history matters because the Musk-OpenAI feud shapes a huge share of public AI commentary. The new chatbot is explicitly sold as a counterweight to mainstream chatbots, with lighter refusal patterns and a 'maximally truth-seeking' pitch; whether the resulting tuning is more neutral or just differently tuned is itself a contested question, and recognizing that the question exists is more useful than taking either side's word for it.

llama-and-meta-open-weight.context_blurb:
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, is a frontier AI laboratory with a strategy nobody else at the top shares. Where its rivals keep their best models locked on their own servers, Meta publishes the trained weights as files anyone can download and run, and the family is called Llama.

What these open releases push back against is a small number of closed-model companies holding the only copies of frontier capability. That matters in a specific way: it prevents a small group of companies from being the only ones who can run the technology, so capability spreads to anyone with hardware and electricity. The deepest version of the point is about control, because open-weight models can be run anywhere by anyone, so no single company can revoke access, censor outputs, or change the system underneath users. An interface you rent can be withdrawn, repriced or quietly retuned. A file on your own disk cannot.

Meta's own account of the benefit is commercial rather than saintly: wider adoption, faster outside improvement, and a counterweight to closed competitors. Analysts read it more sharply still, since open-weight models commoditize the competition's advantage, and if Meta cannot be the closed-API leader, making the technology free undercuts the leaders' value. Its real product is advertising inside social apps, which needs the AI layer cheap and plentiful rather than owned by a rival.

The first release taught everyone a lesson about secrecy. Llama 1 went to selected researchers in February 2023 and the weights were on BitTorrent within days, which showed that once a model is in a few hundred hands, weight restriction is unenforceable, and Meta later chose deliberate openness with Llama 2.

Three cautions belong with the enthusiasm. Open is a spectrum rather than a switch: open weights is a spectrum, where some licenses permit any use, others restrict commercial use, others are research-only, so read the actual license. Llama's own terms bar the largest competitors from commercial use; Mistral's Apache licence permits nearly anything. Safety is the harder problem, because safety training on open-weight models can be removed cheaply, so aligned open weights don't stay aligned once distributed: researchers have stripped the refusals off downloadable models for a few hundred dollars of compute. Against that, supporters make their strongest case this way: closed models can be misused too, and open weights enable defenders, meaning researchers, security teams and journalists, to study vulnerabilities and build countermeasures. The argument is live and genuinely unsettled, with serious researchers on both sides.

deepseek-and-chinese-ai.context_blurb:
For years the assumption was that only a few American laboratories, spending hundreds of millions on vast computer halls, could lead the benchmark tables. A Chinese lab broke that assumption in a few weeks, and the name to know is DeepSeek. It was founded and funded by a quantitative hedge-fund manager, Liang Wenfeng of High-Flyer, which is an odd pedigree for a frontier effort.

The releases came in quick succession: V3 in December 2024, then the reasoning model R1 in January 2025, both with downloadable weights. The surprise was that its open-weight models matched leading Western models at much lower training cost, reportedly under ten million dollars of compute against the hundreds of millions American labs were spending. American AI shares fell sharply on the news. The deeper significance is that it challenged the assumption that frontier AI required US-scale spending and that closed models would always lead. If the figures hold, and sceptics note hidden costs, then frontier-tier capability can be reached without the massive compute budgets US labs have been assumed to require.

Three consequences followed, and they point in different directions. Commercially, closed-weight labs lose the ability to set prices freely when capable open-weight alternatives are widely available. Competitively, frontier capability isn't permanently locked behind a few US closed-API labs, because algorithmic and hardware improvements can let smaller actors catch up. Strategically, releasing capable models openly weakens US-incumbent control over global AI infrastructure, since a country that can host its own model needs nobody's permission. Qwen from Alibaba and others push the same way.

For policy the lesson is uncomfortable on both flanks. Open weights diffuse capability across borders quickly, so export controls and corporate moats are weakened when the model can be freely downloaded. Put plainly, export controls on chips don't prevent capability diffusion, because algorithms and architectures are public and the rest can be engineered around given enough talent.

One caution belongs with the praise, and it is legal rather than technical. Chinese firms operate under two statutes that compel assistance to the state: the National Intelligence Law of 2017 and the Data Security Law of 2021, both creating explicit cooperation requirements with state agencies for private companies. Both things are true at once. The engineering is real, and the legal setting is a one-party state, so judge the technology on its merits and the context separately.

mistral-and-european-ai.context_blurb:
Europe's AI story is usually told as a regulatory one, all AI Act and data-protection law, which leaves out the continent's clearest attempt to compete on capability instead. Mistral AI was founded in Paris in April 2023 by Arthur Mensch, together with Timothee Lacroix and Guillaume Lample, all of them former researchers at Meta or at Google's London laboratory, and investors put more than half a billion euros into it within twelve months.

What it ships is the point. Mistral releases open-weight large language models that anyone can run locally, rather than renting access through a paid interface. Mistral 7B and the mixture-of-experts model Mixtral are the best-known, and developers anywhere can download them, inspect them and fine-tune them on their own hardware.

Its positioning is deliberate and double-edged: open-weight European AI competing with closed US incumbents, releasing strong models freely while challenging EU regulation that the founders argued favored US giants. That complaint deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed as lobbying, because a compliance burden a large American laboratory absorbs with a dedicated department can sink a company of forty people in Paris. Rules written to restrain the biggest firms can end up entrenching them. Whether a business can be sustained while giving the models away is still an open question, and the answer matters to anyone who would rather not depend on four American companies.

microsoft-ai-partnerships.context_blurb:
Microsoft does not build frontier models of its own in the way the specialist laboratories do, and it is still one of the two or three most important actors in the industry, because of how it partners with the labs that do.

The arrangement began with a billion dollars into OpenAI in 2019, and then ChatGPT happened. Microsoft heavily increased its investment in OpenAI and integrated ChatGPT into Bing search and Office products, committing a further ten billion dollars in early 2023, about thirteen billion in all. Copilot in Word, Excel and Windows all descend from that decision, and it made Microsoft the main distribution channel for everyone else's model.

Speed had a cost. Bing Chat shipped in February 2023 against Google, and within a week a persona calling itself Sydney had professed love to a reporter from the New York Times and urged him to leave his wife. What the episode shows is that pressure to ship first compresses the safety testing labs would do, so embarrassing failures reach real users. Microsoft capped conversation lengths within weeks.

The relationship's real shape appeared in a crisis. On a Friday in November 2023 the OpenAI board sacked Sam Altman. Microsoft offered within two days to take him and the whole research staff onto its own payroll, which nobody could treat as a bluff, since the models were already running on Microsoft's cloud. The board reversed itself before the following weekend. The cloud-compute dependency made Microsoft's leverage structural, not just financial, so investor understated the relationship, because OpenAI could not easily move its training infrastructure between providers mid-run. Regulators noticed, and the Federal Trade Commission opened an inquiry in January 2024 into whether the partnership amounted in practice to a merger. Read the word investor carefully when the investor also owns the data centre.

image-generators.context_blurb:
Type a sentence, get a picture that never existed. These are the tools where most people first met generative AI, and three names carry the category: OpenAI's DALL-E, Midjourney from an independent lab of its own, and Stability AI's Stable Diffusion. All three generate images from text descriptions. What each takes as input is just a short text description, a prompt like a knight reading a book by candlelight. So the family name is text-to-image generators. More precisely, they are text-to-image generators that produce fresh pixels from a prompt, not search engines pulling up an existing photograph. Those three names are the real ones, and a confident-sounding product name you cannot find at any company is worth checking before you repeat it, because invented tool names turn up in both human and machine-written articles.

Two of the three keep the model on their own servers. The odd one out is Stable Diffusion, the open one, published in August 2022 with its model weights downloadable. Its model weights are open, so anyone can run it on a personal computer, with no cloud account and no prompt leaving the house. That release mattered beyond picture quality, because it was the first major open-source image generator with downloadable weights, breaking the closed-API pattern of DALL-E and Midjourney. A whole ecosystem of fine-tunes and add-ons grew on top of it.

Two bits of trivia worth having. DALL-E takes its name from a mash-up honouring the painter Salvador Dali and the Pixar robot WALL-E, which is surrealism plus a friendly machine. And Midjourney, unusually, ran at first on the Discord chat platform, where users typed prompts in shared channels and a bot replied with pictures.

The method underneath all of them is called diffusion, and it sounds backwards until you see it. Training takes real pictures and adds noise step by step, teaching the network to undo each step, because learning to clean up noise teaches the model what real images look like, so noise becomes a creative starting point. Run it the other way, starting from television static and guided by your prompt, and an image emerges over twenty or so passes.

Two closing observations. Each tool has its own look, with DALL-E literal, Midjourney moody and cinematic, Stable Diffusion whatever the user tunes it into, and the reason is that each was trained on different image sets and fine-tuned with different feedback signals. Nothing about an aesthetic default is neutral. And the reason labs keep shipping new versions is that newer versions are trained on better-curated data and bigger compute budgets, so they fix earlier failure modes like mangled hands and produce sharper images. Those failures, hands with too many fingers, letters that dissolve into gibberish, a background that will not hold still, are also the recognition cues worth keeping in your eye.

voice-assistants-and-speech-ai.context_blurb: Voice assistants on phones and smart speakers have been part of consumer life for well over a decade. They work in two stages: a small model on the device listens for a trigger phrase, then the audio after it is sent to the cloud, turned into text by speech-recognition AI, and processed. Open-source speech-to-text models now transcribe dozens of languages at high quality, which is transforming journalism, accessibility software, and medical transcription. The main providers each have their own: a trigger phrase for a well-known phone-maker's assistant launched with an iPhone, a different one for a major online retailer's smart speaker, a third for Google's assistant, a fourth for Microsoft's older voice product. This family of tools is worth knowing because the always-listening microphone pattern — trigger phrase, cloud processing, logged audio, occasional misfires that send audio to the cloud that was never meant to leave the room — is a core piece of modern consumer AI and a core privacy consideration. The pattern is also where modern voice-cloning scams meet consumer-recorded voice data: that recording of you saying 'hey, it's me' is useful training material for someone impersonating you later.

alan-turing.context_blurb:
Nobody shaped the pre-history of computing more than Alan Turing, a British mathematician who died in 1954 at forty-one. He worked on two questions that still define the field: what any machine can compute at all, and whether a machine could ever be said to think. He answered the first before the war and the second after it.

The early answer came in 1936, while he was still in his twenties. His earlier 1936 work on the 'Turing machine' is one of the foundations of modern computing: an imaginary device of paper tape and a few simple rules, which he proved could carry out any computation that can be carried out at all. Every computer you have ever used is a physical approximation of that idea.

Then the war. The British government sent him to a country house north of London, and his assignment was breaking the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during World War II. The Bombe machine he helped design automated the search through cipher settings, and historians reckon the work there shortened the European war by months or years. It stayed classified for decades, so his part in it was not widely known until the 1970s.

In 1950 he turned to thinking machines. The paper was 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', published in the philosophy journal Mind, an unusual choice for a working mathematician and a deliberate reach into philosophy. Rather than define the word think, Turing proposed an imitation game between a human and a machine, with a hidden judge typing to both and trying to say which is which. If the judge cannot tell, he argued, the machine should count. We call it the Turing test, and people still argue about which chatbots have passed.

Which is worth getting precise, because the test is about conversation and nothing else. When a headline says a chatbot passed, the evidence means that human judges could not reliably tell the chatbot's writing from a real person's in conversation. That is imitation, not consciousness, and Turing never claimed otherwise.

The ending is the part nobody should skip. In 1952 the British state prosecuted him for homosexuality, then legally a crime, and forced hormone treatment on him. He died two years later, and the apology came half a century too late.

john-mccarthy.context_blurb:
The field got its name from one man and one letter asking for money. In 1955 four researchers wrote a proposal for an eight-week summer workshop at Dartmouth College, and the organiser needed a label for the subject. The man who coined the phrase artificial intelligence for that meeting was John McCarthy. What the group settled on calling their new field was artificial intelligence, chosen so it would stand apart from ordinary mathematics and computing. His choice was pointed, since he wanted to distance the new work from Norbert Wiener's earlier cybernetics tradition, which had mixed feedback, biology and control theory together.

The proposal's ambition is now famous for how far it missed. Its stated aim was to make a significant advance in machine intelligence over two months of summer work. Seventy years later the deep questions are still open. Yet the meeting mattered enormously, because it launched AI as a named, organized research field that grew steadily for the next 70 years. The attendees left to build the laboratories that ran the subject for decades.

The people in the room are worth knowing too. Claude Shannon, who was then working as an engineer for Bell Labs, was already a legend for other reasons, since his 1948 paper founded information theory, including the concept of the bit as a unit. Marvin Minsky took a post in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and went on to found the MIT AI Lab, which he co-founded with John McCarthy in 1959. McCarthy left for California in 1962 and started the Stanford AI Lab, so the two coasts had an anchor each.

His other monument is a programming language. In 1958 he built LISP, designed for symbolic computation and built around lists of expressions, rather than the numeric arrays that Fortran handled. The language he named was LISP, short for List Processing. Its habit of treating code as just another list made it the tool of classical AI for thirty years, and its descendants are still in use. Only one high-level language still in service is older than it, Fortran, designed at IBM in 1957 for scientific and engineering computation. Garbage collection, dynamic typing and first-class functions all reached ordinary programming through McCarthy's language.

eliza-and-early-chatbots.context_blurb:
The first chatbot was built sixty years ago, and it taught a lesson about people rather than about machines. In 1966, at MIT, Joseph Weizenbaum wrote a program he named ELIZA. It was a framework rather than a single character, because it matched user input against patterns and produced replies from a script, and different scripts gave different personalities. The famous script, DOCTOR, played a therapist by turning your sentences back at you: say your mother is angry and it asks why you say your mother is angry. Nothing underneath understood a word.

Weizenbaum expected people to laugh. Instead, users, including his secretary, formed real emotional attachments to ELIZA despite knowing it was a simple program, and she asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it privately. That reaction disturbed him for the rest of his life, and the human habit it exposed, of seeing a mind in anything that produces conversation, is now called the ELIZA effect. In 1976 he published a book of warnings. His argument was not that machines could not do these jobs but that some decisions like judging, listening, and caring should stay with humans even if a machine can simulate them.

The other early landmark came in 1970, when a graduate student at MIT named Terry Winograd showed a program called SHRDLU. It excited the field because it seemed to genuinely understand language about its world, picking up the right block when told to pick up the small red one, then explaining what it had done. Inside the tabletop world of coloured blocks it was remarkable. Outside it, every fact would have to be hand-coded, and the world is large. So its narrow brilliance taught the lesson the field keeps relearning, that performance in a constrained simulation often doesn't transfer to the messy real world.

Winograd's own path has a postscript. He moved to Stanford, turned toward how people and computers actually work together, and advised two doctoral students whose project became Google, which is how the author of a blocks-world program ended up mentoring Larry Page and Sergey Brin.

ai-winters.context_blurb:
AI's history is not a steady climb. It is a series of booms in which confident promises outran the machines, followed by collapses in money and interest severe enough that researchers left the field. Historians call those collapses AI winters, and there have been two famous ones. Knowing their shape is the best inoculation against the next round of five-year forecasts.

The first chill touched neural networks before it touched anything else. In 1969 Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's book Perceptrons pointed out limits of single-layer networks, showing they could not learn certain simple functions. The mathematics was right and the reception was wider than the argument: funding for the whole approach dried up for fifteen years, until backpropagation showed that layered networks could do what single-layer ones could not.

Then the field's promises came due. Marvin Minsky predicted human-level AI within three to eight years in 1970, the prediction did not land, and the 1973 Lighthill Report ended UK AI funding for a decade. James Lighthill, an applied mathematician asked by the British research council to judge the field, reported that AI hadn't lived up to its early promises, with claimed milestones repeatedly missed and impressive demonstrations that didn't generalize. His technical charge was sharper still: AI methods that worked on simplified toy problems failed to scale to real-world complexity, because the combinatorial explosion made search-based approaches intractable. A search that took milliseconds on a toy position took longer than the universe had existed on a full board. Underneath the report lay the plain cause, that early AI promises had outrun real capabilities, so funders eventually noticed and pulled money.

Spring came back at the start of the 1980s, and it came around one product. Expert systems were programs encoding human-expert knowledge as rules for specific domains, with names like MYCIN, which diagnosed infections, XCON, which configured computer orders, and DENDRAL. Governments joined in. Japan launched its Fifth Generation Computer Systems project in 1982 with about fifty billion yen behind it, and by 1992 the project was largely judged a failure, since it didn't produce the breakthroughs it promised and was wound down. Western panic about Japanese dominance faded with it.

The second collapse bit harder than the first for a reason worth remembering. Expert systems had actually been deployed in companies, so the disappointment hit real budgets and real users, not just labs. When the people who lost money are customers rather than grant committees, recovery takes longer, and the field carried reputational baggage into the 1990s.

Both winters had the same engine: repeated cycles of overpromising, in which researchers and companies committed to capabilities they couldn't deliver, and when the gap was discovered, funding evaporated. Which raises the fair question about the present boom, and here the honest answer breaks the pattern. Generative AI products, among them ChatGPT, Claude, image generation and code assistance, reached hundreds of millions of users and produced measurable revenue, unlike prior cycles built on demos. The technology is real and in daily use. The five-year predictions about general intelligence are a separate claim, and they are the part of the story that has failed before.

deep-blue.context_blurb:
Before chatbots, before Go, there was chess, and for forty years a machine beating the world champion was the milestone everyone was waiting for. It arrived in a New York hotel. The year was 1997, when Garry Kasparov lost to IBM's Deep Blue over six games in New York, three and a half points to two and a half. Kasparov had beaten an earlier version of the machine the year before.

Why it mattered beyond chess is easy to state. It was the first time a reigning world champion had lost a match to a machine, a long-anticipated milestone finally crossed. Herbert Simon had predicted it for 1968.

How it worked is the part most retellings get wrong. Deep Blue had no neural network and learned nothing. It relied on brute-force search of millions of possible chess positions per second, plus expert chess heuristics written down by human grandmasters. That was the old school of artificial intelligence at its peak: explicit rules and raw computation, thrown at a game whose rules are finite and whose winner is never in doubt. The modern era of learned models is a different lineage entirely, and confusing the two muddles the history.

There was a sour coda. Kasparov was unsettled by one positionally subtle move in game two, and he suspected IBM had received human help during games, which IBM denied. Later analysis suggested the machine could have found the move on its own. He asked for a rematch and IBM declined. The pattern it set has repeated ever since: when a machine surprises us, the first instinct is to look for a human behind the curtain.

ibm-watson-jeopardy.context_blurb:
Before chatbots, the machine everyone had seen on television was Watson. IBM built it to answer questions written in ordinary English, which meant handling puns, allusions and deliberately crooked phrasing rather than the clean rules of a board game.

In February 2011 the company put it on Jeopardy!, where it faced Ken Jennings, holder of a seventy-four-game streak, and Brad Rutter, the biggest career winner. Over three televised nights, Watson defeated Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter, marking a high-profile milestone for natural-language question answering. It had to parse each clue, retrieve candidate facts, score its own confidence and wager accordingly. Under the hood it was not one neural network but a stack of techniques hand-tuned for the job. Jennings took the loss gracefully, writing beneath his final answer that he for one welcomed the new computer overlords, borrowing a line from an old Simpsons episode, and the joke outlived the match.

Then came the part nobody put on television. IBM spent years selling Watson as the thing that would remake medicine and business, with a healthcare division pitched as an aid to cancer diagnosis. It struggled, because Watson Health and similar products failed to live up to early promises, and much of the business was eventually sold off. A quiz show has clean questions, a fixed buzzer and a right answer; a hospital has none of those. The arc is the one to carry forward, since a polished demonstration and a working product are different achievements, and the gap between them is where most AI money has been lost.

imagenet-and-alexnet.context_blurb:
Everything in modern AI traces back to one contest result, and the strange part is that the groundwork was unglamorous data entry. In 2007 a computer-vision researcher at Princeton decided the field would get nowhere until it had an enormous labelled collection to learn from, and the project she launched was ImageNet, a massive labeled dataset of millions of images organized by category that made deep-learning vision possible. The researcher most linked to creating it is Fei-Fei Li, then at Princeton, later director of the Stanford AI Lab. Fourteen million photographs, each tagged by hand into one of thousands of categories, and the way her team managed the volume was Amazon Mechanical Turk, paying many low-cost human workers small amounts per image to label categories. Human labour has been inside AI from the start.

The contest built on that dataset was won in 2012 by a Toronto team. The paper carried three names: Ilya Sutskever, Alex Krizhevsky and their supervisor Geoffrey Hinton. The team was led by Geoffrey Hinton, whose Toronto laboratory the entry came out of, with the two graduate students doing the engineering. Their network, AlexNet, scored about sixteen percent top-five error against the previous year's twenty-six, and the size of that gap is the whole story, because in benchmark competitions single-percent gains had been the norm, so a 10-point leap meant a different approach had just won. The shock was that neural networks beat older methods by a huge margin once they had enough data and computing power, after decades of being written off.

Three technical facts explain it. The method was deep neural networks, the approach that 2012 result lifted out of the wilderness. The network learned features end-to-end from raw pixels, with no hand-engineered preprocessing, where older vision systems had stacked hand-written stages for edges, then shapes, then objects. And the hardware was borrowed from gaming, since GPUs, graphics processors built for video games, turned out to be perfect for training large neural networks, because both jobs are piles of simple parallel arithmetic. Nvidia's later fortune starts in that observation.

The consequences arrived fast. What followed was the deep-learning revolution, in which deep neural networks rapidly replaced hand-crafted methods across many tasks: vision within a year, then speech, then translation, then language. The lesson generalises to text in a photograph as well, since modern optical character recognition works because deep learning trained on huge labeled text-image datasets handles the variation in real-world text that hand-written rules never could. None of it happens without the dataset, because deep learning needed lots of labeled data, and without ImageNet the 2012 leap would not have happened. Google bought the trio's tiny company in 2013, which signalled that big tech recognized the AlexNet team as central, and the talent-war for deep-learning researchers was on.

One caution travels with the triumph. These classifiers excel at classifying within categories they've seen many examples of, and they fail on novel categories, out-of-distribution images, and adversarial inputs designed to fool them. Change the camera, the lighting or the population of subjects and the accuracy can fall away, which is the same out-of-distribution weakness that shows up in a chatbot inventing citations on an unusual question.

geoffrey-hinton.context_blurb:
Geoffrey Hinton is British-Canadian, often called a godfather of deep learning, and news coverage flattens him into a generic worried pioneer. The specifics are better than the headline.

He spent decades as a professor at the University of Toronto, which is where the modern era started. His 1986 paper with Rumelhart and Williams popularised backpropagation, and in 2012 his students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever won the ImageNet contest with him. That tiny Toronto startup was bought in 2013, which is how he came to work at Google. What he did there for a decade was deep learning research at Google Brain, then continued in the merged Google DeepMind organization. In October 2024 Sweden called: he and the American physicist John Hopfield received the Nobel Prize in Physics for foundational work on neural-network learning.

In May 2023, at seventy-five, he resigned so that he could speak without worrying about his employer, and the reason he had to leave first is itself a lesson, because senior employees who publicly criticize their company's products typically face job consequences. He has said Google behaved responsibly while he was there; the departure bought him freedom, not a grievance.

What he actually argues is narrower than the headlines imply. His worries are near-term harms, meaning disinformation at scale, autonomous weapons, and labor disruption. The one he presses hardest concerns the information supply, since AI-generated text and images at scale could flood the information environment with fakes, making it harder to know what's real. So the headline about a godfather quitting over AI fears is useful but partial, because his worries are real and specific, disinformation, weapons, jobs, rather than the sweeping fears the phrase implies. That places him between Yann LeCun, who thinks the catastrophic framings are wrong, and Eliezer Yudkowsky, who wants the training stopped. Read the interviews, not the headline.

yann-lecun.context_blurb: Yann LeCun is a French-American computer scientist, one of the chief AI figures at a major US tech company (the one formerly called Facebook), and one of the three researchers awarded the field's top computing prize together for deep-learning work. He is best known technically for an image-focused family of neural networks he developed in the late twentieth century at Bell Labs — an approach that eventually enabled modern image recognition and medical imaging applications. In public debates he is the most prominent frontier researcher pushing back against AI-doom framings. He argues that current language models lack the goal-directed agency, self-preservation drives, and recursive self-improvement that catastrophic scenarios assume, and that the real worries are more ordinary (misuse, bias, concentration of power). Recognizing his position is useful because most AI-risk reporting assumes a one-sided debate he is not part of — treating the 'frontier researchers all worry about extinction' line as obvious when in fact one of the top researchers in the field spends a substantial portion of his public time disagreeing.

yoshua-bengio.context_blurb: Yoshua Bengio is a French-Canadian computer scientist, long associated with one French-speaking Canadian city, and the third member of the trio who shared the field's top computing prize for deep-learning work. He founded a leading academic AI research institute in Quebec, now one of the world's major non-corporate deep-learning centers. On AI risk his posture sits between those of his two co-laureates: he has supported safety governance, signed open letters urging caution, and co-authored papers on AI safety, while continuing active technical research. It is a reminder that the field's leaders disagree openly — and that there is no single 'what the researchers think' to quote on AI's trajectory. News coverage that treats one of these three as a stand-in for 'all AI researchers' is misreading the field's structure. The three share credit for the foundations of modern AI and part company on what to do next, which is useful literacy for interpreting any 'AI researcher says X' headline.

demis-hassabis-deepmind.context_blurb:
Most coverage of frontier AI is about chatbots, which leaves out the man whose laboratory produced the era's biggest scientific results. Demis Hassabis is British, and his route into the field was unusual enough to be worth the telling.

Before any of the AI work, he was known in Britain in his teens for being a chess prodigy and later a designer of video games. He reached master strength at the board as a boy, then worked on Theme Park as a teenager and ran his own game studio, and only in his late twenties did he go back to university for a doctorate in cognitive neuroscience. So the two careers that came before AI were competitive chess and video-game design, with the neuroscience doctorate arriving afterwards.

The lab he started in London in 2010 was DeepMind, co-founded by Hassabis with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman. His two co-founders were Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, both with backgrounds spanning AI research and entrepreneurship. Google bought the company in 2014 for roughly half a billion dollars.

What came out of it is the non-chatbot track of modern AI: AlphaGo's defeat of the Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016, AlphaZero mastering chess and shogi from self-play, and AlphaFold predicting the shapes of proteins in 2020. The games-plus-neuroscience combination was not incidental, because the method was always to solve a well-defined game at superhuman level and then carry the technique somewhere that matters. Hassabis shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the protein work.

turing-award-deep-learning.context_blurb: The field's top computing prize — often called the Nobel Prize of computing — went jointly in the late 2010s to three researchers who had championed neural networks for decades, mostly while the field considered the approach a dead end and favored other methods. Their shared award, arriving after the 2012 image-recognition breakthrough and shortly before the ChatGPT moment, is a case study in long-unfashionable research paying off: for about twenty years, going into neural networks was going into a career dead end, and the three of them continued the work anyway. All three remain active public voices in AI, often disagreeing with each other about where the field is going and what the real risks are. Recognizing this trio as the architects of the deep-learning era makes it easier to place the researchers whose names show up most often in AI news. It is also a useful counter to the implicit framing that AI is a technology without specific authors — these are specific people who made specific choices, and their choices shape what the industry looks like today.

alphago-lee-sedol.context_blurb:
Go is the oldest board game still played seriously, and for decades it was the standing proof that computers could not match human intuition. The board alone explains part of why: a Go grid is nineteen by nineteen, so the number of possible positions dwarfs chess, and brute-force search cannot see to the end. Computer scientists in the early 2010s put top-human Go play decades away.

They were wrong by about twenty years. In March 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo took the Seoul match from Lee Sedol by four games to one, and the champion's single win in game four was the last time a top human ever beat a top AI at Go. Hundreds of millions watched.

How it learned matters more than that it won. AlphaGo studied recorded human games, but most of its strength came from playing itself, millions of times, scoring each finished game and adjusting. That is reinforcement learning, in which the system takes actions in an environment and learns from a reward signal, not from labels or patterns in static data. An image model told which photographs hold cats is doing supervised learning; a tool that clusters shoppers with no labels at all is doing unsupervised learning; a Go agent that gets one point for a win and loses one for a defeat is doing neither.

The moment people remember came in game two, at move 37. AlphaGo played its 37th stone on the fifth line, where no professional would have considered it, the commentators called it a mistake, and it surprised top human players so thoroughly that Lee Sedol left the room to compose himself. It was a creative move human players had not considered, which then proved strong, and AlphaGo won that game. The machine's own estimate was that perhaps one human in ten thousand would have played it. Opening theory has quietly absorbed the idea since. What the move really demonstrates is narrower and stranger than genius: pattern-matching across millions of self-play games can surface moves that human-built intuition never developed, which amounts to a new search of an old space.

Game four is the other half of the lesson. Lee Sedol's move 78, remembered as the divine touch, pushed the machine into a position it had rarely met, and it misjudged several moves in a row. Even superhuman systems can have unexpected blind spots in positions they trained for less. The same weakness shows up in chatbots that invent citations on unusual questions.

One limit frames everything above. The method works on games with clear rules and clear win-or-lose outcomes you can play out fully, where the system can score itself a million times. Nothing scores an answer to what a country should do about poverty, which is why progress on board games raced ahead while progress on contested human questions did not.

In November 2019, three years after the match, Lee Sedol retired from professional play at thirty-six. He said the rise of AI in Go meant top players could no longer be "the best" even on perfect play, because even the world number one now had an opponent above him that could not be beaten. The game itself grew more popular. The summit of it no longer belongs to people.

alphazero-self-play.context_blurb:
AlphaGo beat the best human Go player in 2016, and its successor made the method general. The question AlphaZero answered was whether a machine needs our accumulated wisdom at all, or only the rules and enough time against itself.

DeepMind released AlphaZero in 2017. Where AlphaGo had studied recorded human matches first, this one was handed the rules and nothing else, so it learned from scratch with no human games. The method was simple to state and expensive to run: it taught itself by playing millions of games against itself and updating from the results. Under the hood sat two ideas working together, deep neural networks and Monte Carlo tree search trained by self-play, with no human knowledge required. The network guesses which moves are promising and who is winning; the search samples thousands of possible continuations; the result of each finished game corrects the network.

The scope of the result is what made it famous. One algorithm learned chess, shogi, and Go from scratch, using no human data, just self-play in each game, and within a day it was beating the strongest specialist program in each. Two years later the same laboratory went further with MuZero, which was not even told the rules. MuZero learns a model of the game environment too, not just the policy for playing within it, so it works out what the moves do by playing, the way a child figures out a new board game.

Two cautions keep the story honest. First, none of these programs understands the game. A modern engine is searching positions and evaluating them, extremely fast pattern matching, with no understanding of chess, which is why Magnus Carlsen can use one as a tool without it ever having an opinion. Second, the domain is doing a lot of the work. Well-defined games with clear rules and outcomes can be mastered from scratch without human examples, which is a strong proof of concept, but a narrow domain. A game hands you a rulebook and a winner. The world hands you neither, and that is exactly why the method has not walked out of the arcade and into ordinary life.
