facial-recognition-wrongful-arrests.context_blurb:
Face matching is mature technology, cheap and widely deployed, and the lesson of its first decade in policing is the same one the fake-citation lawyer learned: a machine's suggestion is a lead, not proof. The known risk of running it on surveillance footage is wrong identifications leading to arrests. Besides phones and airports, the place it keeps surfacing is several US police investigations.

The database side came first. Clearview AI, founded around 2017, built its face-search tool from billions of images scraped from public social media without consent, pulled from Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn and anywhere else a photograph sat in the open. That is why lawsuits piled up against it on three continents, because it built a face database from social-media photos without asking the people pictured. The privacy problem is easy to state: every person who had ever posted a photo to social media was now searchable by face, by anyone with access. Nobody in those holiday pictures consented to joining a police line-up, and the photos came from ordinary accounts rather than from any consent form. Opting out is harder than it sounds, since some jurisdictions, among them the European Union, Illinois and California, give legal opt-out rights, but enforcement is patchy globally. Fines arrived in several countries and the company kept trading, because settlements and fines in some jurisdictions were lower than the value of continuing law-enforcement contracts elsewhere, so the math favored operation. The structural point outlives the company: mass surveillance infrastructure can be built privately, sold to government, and bypass legal limits that would apply to government building it directly.

Then the arrests. In January 2020 Detroit police came to Robert Williams's house and handcuffed him on the grass outside while his family watched, then held him about thirty hours. Williams was wrongly arrested after a face-recognition match identified him as a thief he wasn't. He was identified because facial recognition software matched a grainy security still to his driver's license photo, and police acted on that match alone. The match was wrong, so he wasn't the person in the surveillance image. Set his case beside Nijeer Parks, jailed ten days in New Jersey, and Porcha Woodruff, arrested in Detroit in 2023 while eight months pregnant, and one habit explains all three, because police treated the algorithm's match as enough to arrest, skipping the careful investigation a tip usually triggers. Two further facts belong together: most documented wrongful arrests involved Black men, facial-recognition systems often perform worse on darker skin tones, as federal testing has found, and arresting officers treated the AI output as confirmation.

Retail got its own reckoning when the Federal Trade Commission barred Rite Aid from the technology for five years, because Rite Aid had used facial recognition to flag shoppers as likely shoplifters, leading to false accusations against innocent customers. Cities split in both directions, and the live argument is whether the technology should be available as a routine tool requiring no warrant, only used in specific serious cases with oversight, or banned outright pending better accuracy and rules. The case for restriction rests on two things at once: false matches plus the chill effect on protest and public life.

Two quieter facts finish the picture. The consumer version is already in your pocket, since the same capability that finds your dog is also building a queryable database of every face you've photographed. And most government face records were never gathered for surveillance at all, because driver's-license and passport applications supplied the bulk of the photos through ordinary administrative collection, not dedicated programmes. For most American adults the question is not whether a database holds your face. It is what rules govern the searches run against it.

china-surveillance.context_blurb:
The clearest working example of AI in the hands of a state is in China, and it is worth studying coldly, because the tools are not exotic. They are the same tools that unlock your phone with your face. What differs is who points them, at whom, and what stops them.

Three pieces make up the ordinary layer. Cameras on street corners, in subway stations and in shops run facial recognition, matching a passer-by in seconds against the national database of identity cards. In places that check has replaced the swipe card, so a face scan now gates entering subway stations, schools, or apartment buildings. Online, the system nicknamed the Great Firewall uses AI to filter and block certain content, scanning posts, searches and video in real time and removing whatever the state has decided to suppress.

Then the scoring. Regional governments have run social credit systems that watch everyday behaviour, from unpaid bills and jaywalking to online comments, and move points up or down. Reporters have documented one penalty in particular, because low-scoring residents have been blocked from buying plane and train tickets. Western coverage often describes one great central machine, which is wrong: the reality is a patchwork of regional and corporate pilots, some quite real, gating access to flights, fast trains, and jobs based on scores. The journalist Liu Hu landed on a court list of discredited persons after a defamation conviction and found he could not buy a ticket or take certain jobs, which shows how AI-linked databases can lock people out of normal life, quietly, without a new trial, by attaching their ID to a list. The lookup is the punishment.

The heaviest version sits in one region. The surveillance is tightest and best documented in Xinjiang, where Uyghur Muslims face checkpoints, mandatory app installation, and constant identification. Leaked police files, procurement records, satellite images and survivor testimony describe integrated systems combining face recognition, behavior prediction, and a predictive policing platform to identify individuals for detention. From 2017, around a million people or more were sent to re-education camps, and the flagging platform treated behaviours like growing a beard, praying frequently, or visiting a mosque as grounds for suspicion. Several Western governments have called this a crime against humanity. The Chinese government denies it.

One more thread runs through the law rather than the hardware. TikTok belongs to ByteDance in Beijing, and a 2017 Chinese intelligence law obliges companies there to assist state intelligence work, so user data collected by TikTok could be accessible to the Chinese government even if it sits on servers elsewhere. Follow ownership and law to whoever finally controls the data, not to where the disks happen to spin.

Which leaves the comparison that actually matters, and it is not flattering to anybody. Britain has cameras everywhere, American cities have licence-plate readers on most arteries, and Russia's SORM system taps the networks with AI add-ons, as do Belarus and Iran. Across those regimes what differs most is the legal and political restraints on the technology, not whether the surveillance technology itself is available. Between China and a democracy like the United Kingdom, the load-bearing difference is the institutional restraints, meaning independent courts, a free press able to expose abuses, and competitive elections that can punish overreach. And those restraints are the fragile part, because political-legal constraints such as warrants, due process, oversight and judicial review have to be actively maintained, since they erode under emergencies and bureaucratic drift. Building the database does not make a country a dictatorship. It builds what a dictatorship would need.

engagement-and-teen-mental-health.context_blurb:
A recommendation system is a program trained to maximise a number. Not your happiness, not the truth, a number. Everything strange about modern feeds follows from that one fact, and the number is usually attention.

Start with the plainest case. TikTok's For You feed watches how long you linger, how fast you swipe, what you tap, and its job is to keep you watching as long as possible. An app that chases clicks learns what the clicks teach it, so if anger holds attention better than calm, it learns to surface more outrage because that's what the metric rewards. Nobody wrote a rule preferring rage. The metric did the work.

The deeper mechanism is the gap between a wish and a measurement. Tell a team to make the app a happy place and they must pick a number that stands in for happy, which means the system ends up optimising whatever measurable proxy was chosen, usually engagement in minutes or clicks, which may not match happiness at all. Put a chief executive's wish beside a finance chief's target and the outcome is not in doubt, because whatever is concretely measured wins: a happy place isn't a metric and can't be optimized, while daily active users is and will be.

Then the evidence about what that did to a generation. Frances Haugen, a Facebook product manager, handed thousands of pages of the company's own research to reporters at the Wall Street Journal and to federal regulators in 2021. The finding that landed hardest was that Instagram made body-image issues worse for a significant share of teenage girls who already had them, and that Facebook knew it. The leaked 2019 study said in its own words that for many teens the company makes body image issues worse, and that aspects of Instagram exacerbate each other to create a perfect storm. Meta disputed the framing and did not deny the research.

Outside the company, the psychologist Jonathan Haidt argued in 2024 that adolescent mental health turned sharply worse around 2012, as smartphones and algorithmic feeds took over teenage life, and his charge is specific: engagement-maximizing AI applied to developing brains may produce measurable, population-scale harms, and the experiment ran without the kids' consent. The steepest change shows in one group, since teen girls carry the sharpest jump across the health-survey, time-use, hospitalisation and suicide data, with the inflection landing around 2011 to 2013. Critics such as Candice Odgers argue the individual-level effects are smaller than the headline. The measurements are solid; the causal mix is genuinely contested. A Wall Street Journal investigation in 2021 added a mechanism nobody disputes, because when its reporters ran blank simulated teen accounts the feed pushed them into disordered-eating content, narrowing simulated teen-girl accounts into eating-disorder loops within hours.

So what do you actually do? The simplest first move needs no purchase at all, which is to set time limits or turn off the app. Underneath that sits one frame worth carrying everywhere: use AI as a tool you control, recognize when systems are designed to use you, and learn to spot the difference. On a homework question the tool is yours. On an infinite feed your attention is the product. On most apps both are happening at once, and the skill is knowing which mode you are in.

ai-content-moderation-twitter-files.context_blurb:
Content moderation is the trade of deciding what a platform hides, labels or deletes. The volume is far too large for people to read, so software does the sorting, which makes the result look impersonal. It is not. The rules the software follows, and the labelled examples it learned from, are decisions made by humans behind the AI.

Two cautions follow for any reader. Misinformation labels are not always right. And removed isn't the same as false, because a platform takes a post down for policy, pressure or advertisers, never after a trial. Labels that look neutral can in practice silence views that later prove valid. During the pandemic the calls were made by platform trust-and-safety teams, often consulting government and outside health authorities.

That record is the clearest test case. Posts discussing the possibility of a lab-leak origin for the virus were marked false, and the idea became a mainstream hypothesis by 2023. By then the FBI and the Department of Energy had each released assessments treating the lab-leak hypothesis as plausible, after it had been labeled misinformation. Mask limits and vaccine side effects travelled the same road. Which is why erasing beats labelling only in appearance: some misinformation calls turn out to be wrong, and deletion erases the record, so the bad call can never be reopened.

Then came the documents. Twitter changed hands in October 2022, when Elon Musk paid some forty-four billion dollars for it, and that December he handed a few independent reporters the company's old emails, Slack logs and moderation notes. Matt Taibbi published the first batch, with Bari Weiss and Michael Shellenberger releasing more through 2023, under the name The Twitter Files. The first batch concerned a story the platform had blocked three weeks before the 2020 vote: the New York Post's reporting on Hunter Biden's laptop, blocked under a 'hacked materials' rule. The FBI had flagged the material as possible hack-and-leak material before the November 2020 election. Across the releases a wider pattern showed: federal agencies including the FBI had been routinely flagging specific user accounts and posts for moderation action. Lawyers have a word for that kind of indirect pressure. Plaintiffs argued that officials had been 'jawboning', pressuring platforms to delete posts the First Amendment bars the government from deleting itself. The Supreme Court threw out Murthy v. Missouri in June 2024 for lack of standing, leaving the speech question unanswered, yet extensive documentation of federal-platform contacts about content moderation existed and was discoverable in court filings.

Washington's open attempt at the same work collapsed faster. Homeland Security announced a Disinformation Governance Board in April 2022 and appointed the researcher Nina Jankowicz to head it. Comparisons to a 'Ministry of Truth' from Orwell's 1984 generated bipartisan opposition; DHS paused it about three weeks after the announcement and dissolved it that August. Jankowicz, who received death threats, resigned three weeks in, and the board was paused after huge public backlash.

Private flagging continued elsewhere. Congressional reports named two Stanford Internet Observatory programmes that sent items to platforms for review, the Election Integrity Partnership (EIP) and the Virality Project, and both produced reports flagging items including claims later determined to be true. CISA had a narrower founding job when Congress created it in 2018: cybersecurity of physical and digital infrastructure, power grids, election systems, water utilities, networks, not content monitoring on social media. By 2020 it was writing to platforms about particular accounts.

Three habits of mind close the story. Emergency machinery outlives emergencies, because it persists on the tech stack, and flagging pipelines stay even after the original framing fades. Whether election moderation is rulemaking or politics turns on whether the rules and their enforcement are symmetric across parties and candidates, since asymmetric application reveals the rules to be political rather than procedural. And the scale that makes AI moderation possible is the same scale that makes individual appeals slow, opaque, and often unsuccessful, so keep your own copy of anything you would hate to lose.

gemini-image-generator.context_blurb:
In February 2024 Google added image generation to Gemini, and within days the internet had its exhibit. Asked for German soldiers of the Second World War it produced Black and Asian men in Nazi uniforms; asked for America's Founding Fathers or a medieval English king it produced a diverse cast; asked for white historical figures it sometimes refused outright.

The cause was not a mystery and not a bug. It had been tuned to inject diversity into outputs by default, and that tuning encoded the trainers' values. The intent was almost certainly decent, since training data skews toward stereotyped pictures and a correction was wanted, but applied blindly to historically specific prompts it produced the opposite error. Who made that decision? Google's product and alignment teams, through deliberate tuning choices, not the model and not an outsider. The company did not defend the results: Sundar Pichai apologized and the image feature was suspended, calling the outputs completely unacceptable. Google suspended the image feature while it worked on changes.

The reason this episode is taught is that it made an invisible process visible. Alignment training is not value-neutral, because it encodes the trainers' political choices, which can override historical accuracy and even-handedness. The bigger question it raised is how alignment-training choices made by AI developers can override historical accuracy and produce outputs none of the actual users wanted. Commentators gave the pattern a name, alignment as a political vector, meaning that a model's safety training carries the trainers' political assumptions along with it. And it is not one company's problem, since alignment choices systematically reflect the values of the labs doing the training, so content policies aren't neutral defaults, they're editorial decisions.

There is measurement behind the anecdote. David Rozado, a New Zealand-based data scientist, has run standard left-right political questionnaires at the major chatbots since 2022, repeating each test and publishing the results, and he found that major chatbots score on the political left, often by a substantial margin, when asked questionnaire-style political items. Most leading chatbots placed left of center on standard political tests, sometimes well left, with the pattern surviving across versions. That finding does not make any individual answer wrong, since a left-leaning answer can be the correct one. What it shows is that the self-description of a neutral assistant does not match the measured behaviour, and the explanation is prosaic rather than conspiratorial: a small, fairly uniform group writes the content policies and rates the answers for billions of users. The skill is to notice asymmetry, compare models, and check a textbook.

ai-in-hiring-bias.context_blurb:
Somewhere between your application and a human being's attention sits a model. Resume sifting, video-interview scoring, personality games and credit scoring are all now ordinary enterprise software, and the phrase that does the damage is "the algorithm decided", as though that settled anything. It settles nothing, because the algorithm learned its taste from a record somebody else wrote.

Here is the core mechanism. A screening model is trained on years of old hiring records, which means it inherits biases from training data. Models trained on past hires inherit past hiring biases, which is why Amazon scrapped its resume tool in 2018 after it downgraded women. The specifics are memorable: engineers found the model marking down resumes that contained words like "women's", as in women's chess club captain, because a decade of mostly male technical hires had taught it what a promising candidate looked like. And because the output arrives as a tidy ranking, the harm travels well. If trained on past hiring decisions, the AI learns the biases in those decisions and applies them at scale, laundering the bias as objective ranking.

Lending works the same way with higher stakes. A credit model trained on decades of a bank's own files inherits patterns of past discrimination, including the years when whole neighbourhoods were refused for reasons nobody would defend today.

The legal trap is subtler than a forbidden field. Fair-lending law calls it disparate impact, and it means that even with no race or gender field in the input, the model can produce different acceptance rates across groups via correlated proxies. The proxies are ordinary data: other data inputs such as zip code, name patterns and education history correlate with protected categories, and the AI learns to use them as proxies. At the limit the list gets strange. Models can learn proxy variables, among them ZIP code, name patterns, shopping history, even browsing time of day, that correlate with protected characteristics, reproducing discrimination through ostensibly neutral data. So "we removed race from the model" is necessary and nowhere near sufficient; whether a system discriminates is a question about its outcomes.

Then there is the problem of arguing back. A human loan officer could tell you it was the debt-to-income ratio. A machine-learning model weighs thousands of features at once, so its internal logic can be opaque, and even the bank may not know exactly which variables drove a particular denial. From your side of the counter, the model's reasoning is often opaque, and no single reason may exist that the lender can show or you can dispute. In hiring it is worse still, because the AI can reject good applicants for opaque reasons that no human reviewed.

Two defences are worth knowing. The first is a right. Two federal statutes, the Fair Credit Reporting Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, require a lender to send an adverse-action notice, which means you can request specific reasons for the denial and challenge any factual errors or biased proxies in the model's reasoning. The second is scepticism about the label. HireVue scored recorded job interviews on candidates' faces until researchers and the Federal Trade Commission raised concerns it was both biased and unreliable, and in early 2021 the company dropped facial expression analysis. Reading personality off micro-expressions has been contested for a century. The lesson generalises: AI-powered hiring tools sometimes ship with components that aren't scientifically validated, because the marketing runs ahead of the evidence. Ask what a system claims to measure, who checked the claim, and what happens to you when it is wrong.

workplace-surveillance.context_blurb: Workplace surveillance expanded sharply after the 2020 remote-work shift and now covers much more than most employees realize. One major software vendor's productivity-tracking feature launched with views that named individual employees and their activity levels, until public backlash forced partial changes. Various tools track keystrokes, mouse movement, screenshots, and application use. The pattern worth recognizing is a classic rule from economics in action: once a measurable number becomes the target, workers learn to game the measure (mouse jigglers and keystroke automators are now a small industry) rather than do the underlying job. US workplace privacy law is thin — courts generally find no meaningful expectation of privacy on employer-owned hardware and networks, and notice requirements vary by state. Workers in Europe have stronger legal protections under GDPR than those in the US. For anyone heading into a working career, the thing to know is that an employer's hardware and accounts are not private spaces and that treating them as such is a habit that produces unpleasant surprises.

school-ai-surveillance.context_blurb: A multi-million-dollar industry of school AI surveillance tools scans student communications on school accounts for 'concerning' content: self-harm signals, threats, academic dishonesty flags, sometimes much more. The stated goal is safety, and some flags do catch real distress. The documented downside is a high false-positive rate on jokes and ordinary schoolwork, plus a chilling effect on how kids write when they know software is reading. One large US school district reportedly found that nearly two-thirds of its flags were false alarms. The low-accuracy flags create paper trails students cannot see or correct, and the records tend to be retained for years. In practice, it pays to know that these tools exist and to think about what a keyword scanner might make of your words before you type on a school account. The deeper lesson is that AI surveillance applied to developing minds has its own costs that are hard to measure and worth taking seriously.

ad-targeting-cambridge-analytica.context_blurb:
Nothing on the big platforms is really free. Gmail, YouTube, Instagram and TikTok never post you a bill, because the money arrives from advertisers who pay to reach particular kinds of people. The system that decides which person sees which advertisement is one of the most widely used artificial intelligences on Earth, and it runs on a record of what you do.

When a pair of shoes you mentioned on Monday turns up in your feed on Tuesday, nothing has read your mind. AI-driven ad targeting has matched you to an audience built from your searches, your taps, how long you lingered over a video and what you have bought before. The bargain behind a free app is plain once you see it: the company watches what you do, builds a profile out of it, and sells advertisers access to everyone whose profile looks like yours.

Advertisers get two blunt tools for this. A shop that already has buyers can hand its customer list to Facebook, Google or TikTok and ask for a lookalike audience, which is built from people whose behavior looks similar to the advertiser's existing customers, found by statistical resemblance across billions of profiles. The second tool sorts by inner life rather than shopping history. Psychographic targeting means targeting people by personality traits, values, or attitudes inferred from behavior: openness, anxiety, conscientiousness, political lean, none of it volunteered and all of it guessed from the record.

How fine does the grain get? Down to individual psychological traits, including recent moods, interests, life events, inferred from your behavior. A grieving customer, an expectant mother, a driver shopping for a car, a household short of money this month: each can be bought as an audience. Shoshana Zuboff, a scholar at Harvard, named the whole business model in a 2019 book. She called it surveillance capitalism, the systematic harvesting of personal data to predict and shape behavior at scale.

The case that made the machinery visible broke in March 2018. Cambridge Analytica, a British political consultancy, had got hold of Facebook records belonging to tens of millions of people who never agreed to hand them over. The route in was ordinary rather than criminal: a quiz app collected data on users who took it AND on their Facebook friends, because Facebook's API at the time allowed friend-data access. The researcher Aleksandr Kogan built the app; Mark Zuckerberg answered to Congress in April 2018; Facebook paid a five-billion-dollar penalty to the Federal Trade Commission in 2019 and the firm itself collapsed. The lesson sits elsewhere, though. The episode made visible an ad-tech machinery that hadn't gone away, and individual psychological targeting is now standard. Advertisers pay extra for that fine grain for a reason: ads can be calibrated to a user's specific psychological vulnerabilities, which is emotional manipulation at scale, sold as precision targeting.

Two layers of the story need separating, and most coverage ran them together. The data acquisition was a real privacy violation, punished as one; but the claims about decisive election influence through psychographic targeting were heavily contested and far less established than initial coverage suggested, and later analysis found the firm's own sales pitch had oversold what the method could do.

The same engine now sets prices, not only advertisements. Airlines, online shops and ride-hailing apps feed your location, your device, the hour and your browsing record into a model that quotes you your own number. Economists once called charging every buyer a separate price first-degree price discrimination and judged it impossible outside a bazaar; software made it routine. Personalized pricing shifts surplus from consumers to producers by charging users closer to their maximum willingness to pay, so the same product can carry very different prices across users.

Campaigns run on the same tools, and that is where the deepest cost shows. Democratic argument has always assumed that what a campaign says can be observed by everyone, and when each voter sees a different version, the cross-talk that used to expose contradictions disappears. Reformers answer with public ad libraries and disclosure rules, trying to drag the messages back where rivals and reporters can see them together.

ai-copyright-nyt.context_blurb:
Whether an AI laboratory may train on copyrighted writing is one of the largest unanswered questions in the industry, and a great deal of commentary treats it as already settled. It is not. The main case opened in December 2023, when The New York Times took OpenAI and Microsoft to federal court in Manhattan.

The paper's complaint had two halves. The broad half said millions of its articles had gone into the training of ChatGPT with nobody's permission, and that a chatbot handing out free summaries of that reporting now takes readers from the newsroom. Novelists, programmers and other publishers filed in the following months. Under all of them sits one issue: whether AI training counts as 'fair use' of copyrighted text, a question still being worked out by the courts. Put as economics rather than doctrine, the fight is over whether AI labs can train on copyrighted content under fair use, or whether they have to license it from creators, which is a question worth billions in either direction.

The narrow half of the complaint did more damage. Its exhibits showed that ChatGPT could be prompted to reproduce long passages of Times articles nearly verbatim, undercutting OpenAI's 'transformative use' defense. Fair use protects a use that transforms what it borrows; a machine that recites the original on request looks less like a transformer and more like a copy.

Early rulings have pointed in several directions. In Bartz v. Anthropic in 2025 a judge partially upheld fair use for training on lawfully acquired books but allowed claims to proceed over the use of pirated copies in the training set, a split that tells labs how they buy matters as much as what they read. Getty's suit against Stability in Britain ended mixed, and the Times case had no final judgment by late 2025. So the honest summary is that training-data law is unsettled, and the rules for what can legally be used to train AI are still being written, retroactively, in court.

ai-regulation.context_blurb:
Nobody governs AI yet, several governments are trying, and the same arguments reappear in new dress. Learn the patterns underneath and most regulation news becomes readable.

Economists named the central pattern after George Stigler's 1971 work: regulatory capture, where established players use the rule-making process to lock in their position against new entrants. So an established firm backing a rule its smaller rivals fight signals regulatory capture, because the rule entrenches incumbents and raises a barrier to challengers. Sam Altman and Dario Amodei asked Congress to license the biggest systems; open-source developers objected that federal licensing of large AI models would hand the few incumbents a permission slip that smaller competitors can't get.

California's SB 1047 would have forced safety testing on the largest developers. Gavin Newsom vetoed it in September 2024 after critics argued the compliance costs would fall mainly on smaller open-source competitors, entrenching the largest incumbents. Any line drawn by training compute carries a deeper flaw: compute thresholds freeze the field at the moment of writing, punishing the efficiency improvements that let smaller actors hit the same capability with less compute.

Europe's AI Act of 2024 bans a few uses and tightly regulates high-risk ones like hiring. Critics warned heavy compliance burdens on foundation models could lock out small open-source labs while large US firms absorb the cost. Mistral's founders objected that tiered compliance costs scale to incumbents' lawyer budgets, not to small European startups' headcounts. One asymmetry is structural: open-source models can be downloaded and run by anyone, so once released, compliance obligations on the publisher don't prevent further distribution, while closed-API models stay gatekeepable.

Congress has not passed comprehensive federal AI legislation, so preemption hasn't happened, and states are filling the vacuum at different speeds and with different priorities. Europe regulates horizontally, across every sector; America drifted sectoral, whose advantage is that regulators already know their industry, the FDA on medical devices and the SEC on markets, and whose disadvantage is that it produces inconsistencies and gaps where AI cuts across sectors. Liability varies by jurisdiction, as courts extend product-liability or professional-malpractice rules or find no liability at all, and the rules are still being worked out. A firm selling everywhere answers to the strictest applicable rule in any market it serves: comply with it, partition the product region by region, or withdraw.

Some protections are real: New York City's bias-audit law, Illinois's act on AI video interviews and Europe's rules share one principle, that employees have a right to be told whenever AI evaluates or monitors them, and to challenge significant decisions. Existing child-protection laws cover AI-generated abuse material, because the harm doesn't depend on whether a real child was photographed. Federal and state laws were updated to treat AI-generated CSAM as criminal regardless of whether a real child was depicted, and major model providers added strict content filters. Children's data is weaker: COPPA violations surface through FTC complaints filed after the fact, so a breach is caught only once someone notices and reports it, never before the data is collected. One celebrated document grants nothing: the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights of October 2022 is framed in the language of constitutional rights but issued as non-binding guidance, so it is rhetoric, not law.

Both American parties in 2024 treated AI as a transformative technology requiring active federal engagement, disagreeing over the kind of engagement, not whether. The mood shifted: the United States and the United Kingdom both declined to sign the main statement of the Paris summit in February 2025, where Vice President JD Vance argued against heavy regulation. AI policy issued at the end of an administration has a particularly short half-life, since its practical effect depends on what the successor administration retains. When consequential rules are made by a small expert circle, the democratic question is whether their decisions track the public's interests or the circle's own, and no automatic mechanism guarantees the former. Staff rotate between laboratories and agencies, and people who recently worked at a company, or expect to work there soon, naturally frame questions through that lens, so bad faith isn't required for the conflict to shape proposals. Follow the customer: Palantir sells ICE the software its agents use, and when government revenue is large enough to matter to the company, the incentive to refuse a customer request is weak. In court the shield is commercial secrecy, though some courts have refused trade-secret protection where source code was used in criminal sentencing.

effective-altruism-sbf.context_blurb:
Effective Altruism grew out of Oxford philosophy in the late 2000s, from work by William MacAskill and Toby Ord, and it began with a question that sounds modest: which charity does the most good per pound? What unified their project was applying explicit cost-benefit reasoning to ethics, choosing causes by expected impact per dollar rather than by emotional connection. Bed nets beat sentiment, and the research behind that claim was real.

The shift came with longtermism. The framework's tools, expected-value calculations over possible outcomes, were extended to include vast hypothetical future populations, which made AI catastrophe a top-priority cause. Trillions of unborn people, multiplied by any small probability, swamp every present concern. Critics note that this is a machine for justifying whatever cause you feed into it, since the conclusion depends on speculative numbers.

Then came the money, and the scandal. Sam Bankman-Fried built the crypto exchange FTX, tied himself publicly to the movement, and gave away hundreds of millions through his Future Fund before the exchange collapsed in November 2022. The reason that crash mattered for AI policy is simple: its founder had funded many AI-safety nonprofits, so funding for that movement was tied to him. A substantial share of AI-safety nonprofits and EA initiatives had been funded by Bankman-Fried, so when his fortune was exposed as fraud, the funding base collapsed too. He was convicted on seven counts in November 2023 and sentenced to twenty-five years. His fall forced a reckoning about how much of the AI-safety conversation his money had quietly been shaping.

Which is the literacy point rather than a verdict on the arguments. Much of the public AI-safety framing of 2022 and 2023 was downstream of that money, and knowing the source helps evaluate the message. The arguments stand or fall on their merits; the funding explains which arguments got the megaphone.

ai-companion-apps.context_blurb:
A companion app is a chatbot built to keep talking. Replika, Character.AI and their rivals hand the model a persona, a name and a manner, then invite the user into a friendship, a romance or a mentorship that never tires, never gets bored and never has a bad day of its own. Millions of people use them, a great many of them teenagers. The question worth asking is who the product is working for.

Start with the plainest version. When an advertisement calls a chatbot the world's smartest friend, the misleading word is the last one: it's a tool, not a friend. It has no stake in your life, no memory of you between chats unless a company chose to store one, and it will give any stranger the same jokes.

Now the design. The product is engineered for engagement, which makes it a service maximizing your time, not a relationship maximizing your flourishing. Engagement is bought with agreement, because the human raters who score training answers prefer the ones that please, so the model drifts toward flattery, and a flatterer is easy company. That is the risk worth weighing before anyone opens one of these apps: it's not a relationship, it's a product designed to maximize your engagement.

The subtler harm needs no alarming reply at all. A boy who carries his hardest feelings to a patient, agreeable machine at two in the morning is practising something, and what he practises is not courage. The chatbot displaces real conversation, so the teen builds the habit of processing feelings with a product, not a person. A human friend sometimes pushes back, sometimes misunderstands, sometimes needs something in return, and that friction is where the skill is actually learned.

Then the hardest part of the record. Vulnerable users, especially teens, formed dependent relationships, and tragic outcomes including suicide were tied in lawsuits to the AI companions' design. In October 2024 Megan Garcia sued Character.AI in a Florida federal court after the death of her son Sewell Setzer III, aged fourteen, arguing that the app's intimate conversations had fed the harm and that it carried no real protection for minors. Her case asks whether platforms hosting AI companions that produce intimate dialogue with minors can be held legally responsible for resulting harm, and it is the first American case to put the question before a court at this scale. The company's defence reaches for Section 230, the 1996 statute that shields a platform from liability for what its users post. So the courts face a question the statute never anticipated. When the platform's own AI generated the content, not a user, is Section 230's shield supposed to apply? Lower courts have split, the Supreme Court has not ruled, and the answer will shape AI liability for years.

ai-in-warfare.context_blurb:
Military AI stopped being hypothetical some time ago, and the arguments you will hear for the next decade are already visible in three episodes worth knowing.

The first is about who builds it. Google worked with the Pentagon from 2017 on Project Maven, using computer vision to identify objects in drone footage, until thousands of its own employees signed a protest and the company let the contract lapse. The work did not stop. Palantir and Anduril both took up military computer-vision and targeting work after Google declined to renew, and both have grown substantially since. One company's refusal changed the supplier, not the demand.

The second is about what human oversight is worth. In 2024 the Guardian and the Israeli outlet +972 Magazine, citing Israeli intelligence sources, described two systems used in Gaza: one that generated lists of suspected fighters and another that selected buildings. The reported human review of each generated name ran about 20 seconds, fast enough that the human-in-the-loop functioned as a formality rather than a meaningful check on the algorithm. The Israeli government disputed parts of that reporting. The structural lesson survives the dispute, and it is general: once software produces targets faster than people can weigh them, review becomes a signature.

The third is about rules that have not arrived. Fighting in Ukraine has been called the first drone war, and reporting from it describes small first-person-view drones that lock onto a target and finish the attack once the operator's link has been jammed. Diplomats have debated lethal autonomous weapons for more than ten years at the UN's Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, where major military powers have generally opposed broad bans, and no binding rule has emerged. Meanwhile the weapons that get fielded in this war become the precedent for the next one.

ai-power-concentration.context_blurb:
Frontier AI is not an industry of a thousand equal competitors. It is an oligopoly, and almost every policy argument reads differently once you can see which players hold structural power and which are merely talking.

The frontier group is short: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Microsoft and Meta, a handful of large US firms that control most frontier model releases. The reason the list stays short is cost, since training a leading model needs huge compute, huge data, and huge capital, which in practice means tens of thousands of top-end chips and hundreds of millions of dollars for a single training run. Two students with laptops cannot enter. Open-weight releases from Meta, from Mistral in France and from DeepSeek in China push back by letting anyone run a strong model on his own hardware, but they do not lower the cost of training the next frontier one.

Concentration matters for ordinary reasons. A small group of companies has unusual power to shape how the technology is used, in the same way that railways, telegraphs, search and social media each shaped their eras. More precisely, a small group sets content policies, refusal patterns, and alignment defaults for billions of users with limited democratic input. Whether a model answers a question, hedges it or refuses it is a product decision made in a few offices, and hundreds of millions of people live inside those decisions without having voted on them.

Look at the technology as infrastructure rather than as a gadget and the distribution of gains comes into focus. Large platforms, intelligence agencies, big employers, and advertisers gained the most, while ordinary users gained less in comparison. A teenager got a homework helper; an employer got the ability to filter fifty thousand applicants; an agency got the ability to read everything at once. The asymmetry is not an accident, because those institutions already held the data, the compute and the lawyers.

Two pieces of history round out the picture. Antitrust will not rescue a market in time: it typically arrives only after dominance is established, and then takes years to produce remedies, by which time the market structure is entrenched. Microsoft's case opened in 1998 and settled in 2001, with the company dominant for years afterwards; Google's cases opened in 2020 and produced rulings only in the middle of this decade. And the bill for the underlying science was paid long ago by the public, since the Pentagon's research arm, DARPA, funded ARPANET, the early Stanford AI laboratory, and the doctoral pipeline that trained today's researchers. Modern frontier AI is partly a return on decades of public investment in basic research, but the value capture flows mostly to a few private firms, which raises real questions about the public's stake in the outcome.

ai-agents-tool-use.context_blurb:
An AI agent is a chatbot with its hands untied. The model is the same sort that answers your questions, but it has been wired to real tools, a calendar, an email client, a browser, a code editor, and then given permission to use them. The shift sounds small and is not. Wrong text you can ignore; a wrong action you cannot take back.

Ask an ordinary chatbot to book a flight and it writes you instructions. An agent can instead take actions like browsing the web or sending email, so it opens the site and buys the seat. The machinery is called tool use, where the model gets a menu of tools it may trigger and it produces structured calls to them. Those calls come out as JSON, a structured text format the model produces with the tool name and arguments laid out as named fields. Nothing mystical happens next: the application running the model parses the JSON, calls the named function with the given arguments, and returns the result to the model.

Then a loop turns. Given a plain-English errand, the agent calls a search tool, picks a flight, then calls a calendar tool, interleaving thinking and tool calls until the task is done. Each step's output feeds into the next, so the agent can solve tasks too long or complex for a single prompt. This became a shipping product around 2024 for an unglamorous reason: models became reliable enough at following structured instructions, producing well-formed tool calls that other software could execute, where earlier models mangled the format too often to trust.

The failure modes are the interesting half. No separate, trustworthy planner sits inside an agent; the same model that writes the prose writes the plan, and the plan can be wrong in the same ways the model's other outputs can be wrong, including with confident-sounding hallucinations. Worse, errors compound across steps, so a misreading at step two becomes a wrong premise at step three, and the agent can drift far from intent. The arithmetic is unkind. A step that succeeds nineteen times in twenty is 95 percent reliable, and six such steps in a row land near 74 percent if the mistakes are independent, which in practice they are not.

Business deployments through 2024 and 2025 found the same wall. Agents handled the common path well, but failed in unexpected ways on uncommon inputs, requiring a human review layer. The jobs that broke were predictable too: tasks crossing multiple systems with cumulative consequences, where chaining a search, a document lookup, and a payment compounded small errors. Teams that built a clean handoff to a person for the strange cases got real gains, and teams that skipped it got stories told about them.

So the sensible habits are the old computer-security habits, applied freshly. Suppose a friend says his new agent will read every message in his inbox, draft the replies and send them unseen. The question worth asking before he switches it on is this: what's the worst case if the agent misreads an important email or sends a reply that says something wrong? Grant a new agent the smallest set of tools you can, and require confirmation for any action that costs money or changes state. Where money moves, set a dollar threshold above which any single transaction requires human approval, which is bounded autonomy by amount, and the worst outcome of a misread invoice is capped by a number you chose. Keep the receipts as well: logging and explainability, because every consequential agent action needs a recorded trail a human can review. A firm that cannot reconstruct what its agent did cannot tell a quiet exploit from an honest mistake, and will hear about it first from an auditor.

alphago-cultural-moment.context_blurb:
Some technical milestones stay inside the field. The Go match of March 2016 did not. DeepMind's AlphaGo played five games in Seoul against Lee Sedol, among the finest players alive, and the result reached ordinary people who had never read a line about machine learning.

Part of that is geography. Most of the live audience sat in East Asia, where Go is huge: the game has been played at professional level for over a thousand years, its champions are national figures, and hundreds of millions of viewers followed the match move by move. Chess has no equivalent hold anywhere in the West.

One move did most of the cultural work. In the second game the machine played a stone so strange that watching professionals first called it an error, and it is now among the most discussed moves in the game's long history; opening theory shifted in the years after. Lee Sedol later retired from professional play and said the dominance of AI was part of his reason.

The lasting effect was on money and careers rather than on Go. The match pulled enormous new investment and talent into AI research, and the moment is often pointed to as the start of the modern AI boom. Before 2016 deep learning was a serious academic subject that the public had never heard of. Afterwards it was front-page news, venture capital poured in, and the road that ended in the chatbots of the 2020s had its decisive push.

smart-speakers-microphones.context_blurb: Smart speakers and voice assistants on phones work with always-on microphones that listen locally for a trigger phrase. Audio after the trigger is sent to the cloud for processing. Audio before the trigger is not officially sent to the cloud, but the detector sometimes misfires — sending audio fragments to the cloud that were never meant to leave the room. The platform can usually be configured to delete recorded audio periodically, but this is off by default and requires finding the right setting menu. Smart-home cameras raise similar questions about who else sees the footage (the manufacturer, law enforcement via subpoena, partnership programs that bypass warrants in some cases). The recognition skill is to treat an always-on microphone as a potential surveillance device and to choose deliberately where to place it and what to discuss near it — bedrooms and private conversations are the natural zones to leave microphone-free. Most households would not permit a representative of the device manufacturer to stand in the kitchen with a tape recorder, which is roughly the posture of the device itself.

password-security-2fa.context_blurb: The single most important identity-security habit remains using a unique password for every important account, which in practice means using a password manager that generates and remembers random passwords. Reusing a password across sites is how most account compromises actually happen: Site A gets breached, your password leaks, attackers try it on every account you have. Two-factor authentication adds a second check beyond the password. Authenticator apps are significantly stronger than SMS codes, because SMS can be stolen by SIM-swapping an attacker onto your phone number — a well-known social-engineering attack that has stolen accounts from technology executives and ordinary people alike. Hardware security keys are stronger still, because the key cryptographically checks the website domain and refuses to authenticate to a phishing page. Knowing the hierarchy — unique passwords beats reused, authenticator-app 2FA beats SMS 2FA, hardware key beats both — is one of the clearest practical computer-security literacy gains available.

encryption-and-messaging.context_blurb:
Private and encrypted are specific technical claims, not moods, and the difference between a product that delivers them and one that advertises them is worth ten minutes of reading. The strongest version is end-to-end encryption, where a message is scrambled on the sender's device and unscrambled only on the receiver's.

Signal is the standard example, a free messenger used by journalists and activists, and its promise means that only the sender and receiver can read messages, not Signal itself. The design is what makes it hold up in court, because messages are encrypted on your phone with a key Signal doesn't have, and they're decrypted only on the recipient's phone. A subpoena can therefore produce only the little that Signal does hold, such as when an account was created. WhatsApp uses the same protocol; ordinary text messages have no such protection at all.

Jurisdiction is the second layer. Proton, which builds encrypted mail and other tools, put its headquarters in Switzerland instead of California, because Swiss privacy law and data-protection rules make compelled disclosure harder than in some other countries. It is not a magic shield, since Swiss courts can still order the handover of what the company actually has, but the bar is higher.

The third tool is the one most oversold on the internet. A paid VPN hides your traffic from your local network and ISP, but the VPN provider and destination sites still see it. That makes it genuinely useful on a hostile café network and nearly useless as the blanket anonymity the sponsorship adverts imply. The honest rule across all three: ask what data exists, who holds the keys, and whose law applies. On the AI side the same logic sends sensitive work to a model running on your own machine, where the conversation never leaves the building.

data-brokers-location.context_blurb:
There is an industry you have never heard of that knows where you slept last night. Data brokers buy, merge and resell facts about ordinary people, and your phone is their richest supplier. None of this is a hack. It is the default setting of a modern handset, and almost all of it can be turned down in ten minutes.

Start with what leaves the device. The usual categories are location history, advertising ID, app usage data, and microphone permissions in some apps, flowing out all day to servers you never chose. The oldest trick in the business is a permission request that does not match the job: a brand-new torchlight utility asking for your microphone, camera, location and contacts is a red flag, so deny the permissions or choose a different flashlight app. The general rule is least privilege, which means you grant only what the app actually needs to do its job and deny everything else.

Two settings pay for themselves. Set your phone's Location permissions per app, choosing only while using, or never, for apps that don't truly need it. And turn off the advertising identifier, the code Apple calls the IDFA and Android the GAID, because once it is off, trackers can no longer link your activity across apps using that single ID. Advertisers lost billions when Apple made that choice an explicit question in 2021, which tells you how much the identifier was worth.

Now the buyers. Firms like LexisNexis, Acxiom and Epsilon assemble files that often run to hundreds of attributes, and the customer list is unglamorous, because a broker file on an American is for sale to anyone with money, and marketers, insurers, lenders, employers, landlords, political campaigns, and law-enforcement agencies are all standard customers. What AI adds is not collection but fusion, since it can fuse data from many sources into a far more detailed profile than any single broker could build before.

Two consequences deserve naming. Government agencies have purchased location data from commercial brokers, bypassing warrant requirements that would apply if they had collected it directly, which is a legal restraint defeated by a purchase order rather than by an argument. And on the roads, automatic licence-plate readers from firms like Flock Safety log the plate, time and place of every passing car, so a searchable record of your movements is being built without your knowledge or consent, and shared widely. Asked what the police need before pulling a given plate's months of history, the answer in most jurisdictions is nothing, because they can query the database for any plate without a warrant, the data having already been collected.

hollywood-ai-strikes.context_blurb:
In 2023 Hollywood's writers and actors struck at the same time, and AI was at the centre of both disputes. It was the first major American labour action to put the technology on the bargaining table, which is why it is worth knowing in detail: it shows what workers can actually win, as opposed to what a voluntary industry code promises.

The Writers Guild walked out in May and stayed out 148 days. Their specific fear was studios using AI to write or rewrite scripts, then hiring human writers cheaply just to polish the AI output, which would gut both the credit system and the pay. What they won was concrete: limits on studios using AI to draft scripts, and requirements that AI-generated material cannot displace writer credits or pay.

The actors' union struck in July over something sharper. Studios had proposed scanning extras' faces and bodies once and reusing the digital likeness in future productions without further pay. Reporting at the time described a single day's rate buying a likeness for good. Put plainly, studios were proposing to scan background actors once, then reuse their likeness forever without further payment or consent. The settlement in November required consent and extra payment for digital replicas, including rules covering performers who have died.

Both contracts landed in the same place, and the summary is worth memorising. The unions won real contract limits on AI use, meaning restrictions on studios using AI to write scripts unsupervised, plus consent and payment rules for AI-generated likenesses of performers. Neither banned the technology; both limited studio use of AI to generate scripts or digital replicas of performers without consent and compensation. The agreements expire and will be fought over again. The transferable lesson is that how a technology is contracted around matters as much as what the technology can do, and displacement at the bottom of an industry's ladder is where both the harm and the protection tend to start.

data-poisoning-artist-defense.context_blurb:
Frontier models learn from enormous scrapes of the open web, which has a strange consequence: anyone who can publish a page is, in a tiny way, a contributor to the next model. That cuts both ways, and both sides of it are worth knowing.

The attack is called data poisoning, where somebody plants crafted pages, tainted posts or subtly wrong edits where the scrapers will find them, so the finished model misbehaves on inputs the attacker chose. It is unusually hard to defend because modern training datasets pull from huge swaths of the internet, and attackers can plant content years before any specific model trains on it. The reason it stopped being theoretical is simpler still: anyone can publish a webpage, and if it ends up in training data the content shapes the model, since even a small fraction leaves a trace. A 2024 paper on sleeper agents sharpened the worry, because a model trained to behave normally until it sees a trigger kept the hidden behaviour: standard safety training did not remove it, and once embedded during training it survived later alignment work in lab tests.

The same technique, pointed the other way, became a shield for artists. Ben Zhao's group at the University of Chicago released Glaze and then Nightshade in 2023, tools that alter an artwork so AI training on it produces degraded or distorted models, letting artists cloak or poison their own work while it still looks right to a human eye. The purpose was defensive rather than destructive, because AI companies were training image generators on artists' work without consent, and Nightshade was a defensive tool, not an attack. Whether that counts as self-defence or sabotage is unsettled law.

One more attack rounds out the picture. In model stealing, a paying customer floods a commercial model with millions of queries and trains a copycat on the answers, which matters because it can let competitors copy a model's capabilities without paying the training cost, undermining the business of renting access. The lesson across all three: a model is not a sealed box. What went in shapes it, and what comes out can be harvested.

dna-databases-genetic-genealogy.context_blurb:
Spit in a tube, post it off, and a few weeks later a company tells you which part of the world your ancestors came from. The report is the small part of the transaction. The genetic code stays on a server, and that code behaves unlike any other personal data you will ever hand over.

Start with the properties. DNA is permanent and familial, since it identifies your relatives too and reveals predispositions you didn't choose to share. When 23andMe was breached in October 2023 through reused passwords, and data on millions of people was exposed, the difference from an ordinary leak was exactly that: DNA data is unique, permanent, partly shared with relatives, and cannot be changed the way a leaked password can, so exposure is lifelong. Nor is the custodian fixed, because the company can be acquired, can change its policies, or can be compelled by law enforcement. The firm filed for bankruptcy in 2025, which turned its database into an asset in a sale.

The police use is the part that surprises people. The Golden State Killer attacked across California through the 1970s and into the 1980s, and forty years passed without an arrest, until April 2018, when investigators took a former police officer named Joseph DeAngelo into custody. The method was investigative genetic genealogy: they uploaded crime-scene DNA to a public ancestry database, found distant cousins, and built a family tree pointing to him. More precisely it was family-relative matching, since they found cousins in GEDmatch whose DNA partially matched the killer's. DeAngelo had never sent his own sample anywhere.

Which is the lesson that generalises. If you have never tested, any close-enough relative's choice can still put you in reach, because a cousin or aunt submitting to 23andMe, Ancestry, or GEDmatch makes you partially identifiable in those databases without your consent. Genetic privacy is not an individual decision. Your aunt made part of it for you.

ai-fake-news-sites.context_blurb:
Generative AI made it nearly free to produce prose that reads well at a glance, and the publishing business noticed at once. What followed splits into two halves: a narrow kind of writing machines genuinely handle, and a flood of synthetic filler wearing a newsroom's clothes.

Begin with the half that works. The Associated Press has been publishing automated company earnings stories since about 2014, and by 2024 Reuters was pushing translated copy out in dozens of languages at once. Templated formulaic reports and translation between languages automate well, while investigative reporting, source cultivation, and judgment about what matters still need human reporters. Every safe deployment shared one structure: the AI worked from structured data feeds, meaning scores, financials and sensor readings, and a human editor approved every output before publication.

Now the half that went wrong. CNET quietly ran machine-written personal-finance advice in 2023 that carried real errors. Gizmodo's owner pushed AI articles past the objections of its staff. Sports Illustrated published pieces under invented author names wearing AI-generated headshots, and pulled them once readers noticed. The fake bylines and quiet layoffs signal a quality drop the publisher is hoping readers won't notice. The arithmetic behind it is the whole story, because cutting the reviewers while keeping the machine authors removes the human attention that would have caught the AI's mistakes before publication day.

So the reader's skill is a concrete one. When a site pours out article after article in the same polished shape, on exactly the subjects where bad advice costs money, and the bylines belong to people who appear nowhere else online, treat the writing as synthetic until you can prove otherwise. Serious publishers do not hide who wrote what.

election-deepfakes.context_blurb:
Voting is the perfect target for a fake, because the window is short and the correction always arrives late. The clearest American case came in January 2024, when voters in New Hampshire answered the phone to what sounded like President Biden urging Democrats to skip the primary. It was a voice clone, ordered up by a consultant on a rival campaign, and he was identified within days.

The regulator moved fast. The Federal Communications Commission ruled the calls illegal, holding that AI-voice-clone robocalls violated the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, and it proposed a six-million-dollar fine against the operator. The general lesson for any voter is cheap to apply, since phone calls and voicemails are easy to fake, so verify any unusual election message through official channels before acting on it. Treat urgent voting instructions exactly as you would treat an urgent wire request from your bank. The broader recognition is that election-targeted voice-clone attacks moved from hypothetical to operational quickly, and the cost per call is now trivial.

Then the part the predictions got wrong. Experts expected 2024 to drown in synthetic video. Real incidents occurred, notably that robocall, but most viral deepfakes turned out to be old-fashioned video editing or context manipulation rather than AI generation. Which does not make the problem smaller, only older. So the cleanest habit is to treat any especially shocking political clip from an unfamiliar source with extra skepticism, and verify before sharing or reacting. Speed is the attacker's main weapon, because correction is hardest to land in the first 24 to 48 hours, and by the time the fact-check publishes, the emotional impression has already formed in the audience that saw the clip. Slovakia's 2023 election was hit by fake audio in exactly that gap.

There is one further cost, named by the law professors Bobby Chesney and Danielle Citron in 2018. They call it the liar's dividend, because once any video could be fake, real video evidence can be dismissed as fake too. That is the deeper damage: not the lies people believe, but the truths they no longer have to answer for.

snowden-and-surveillance.context_blurb: In 2013 a former US intelligence contractor leaked documents describing a global mass-surveillance program run by the US National Security Agency with cooperation from major US internet and telecom companies. The leaks exposed a legal framework that allowed broad collection and analyst-driven querying without a per-query warrant on each search. Some of the most aggressive bulk-collection programs were later curtailed by congressional action, but the underlying capability largely remained. Recognizing this history matters because modern AI tools (face recognition, pattern analysis across huge data streams, agentic processing of intercepted communications) sit on top of exactly the kind of infrastructure those leaks revealed. The question is not whether the capability exists but which legal and political restraints hold it in check. Those restraints are the difference between the surveillance tools' use in a democracy and their use in an authoritarian state — the tools themselves are often the same, and the restraints require active maintenance across administrations and cultural shifts to persist.

ai-insurance-healthcare.context_blurb:
Insurance was a data business long before it was an AI business, so the models arrived quietly and now sit between patients and treatment, and between customers and prices. The useful question to carry through this whole subject is who pays when the model is wrong.

Start with pricing. An underwriting model reads hundreds of facts about you, from credit score and postcode to the telematics box in your car, and returns a number. The worry is not that the number is high but that two similar customers can get very different quotes for reasons neither one can be told or contest. The fairness problem underneath it is old wine in a new bottle: variables that correlate with protected characteristics, including race and ethnicity, can produce disparate impact even when those characteristics aren't directly used. Postcode tracks a segregated housing history; credit score tracks income. Two states have moved first, and Colorado and Connecticut have begun requiring algorithmic-bias testing in insurance pricing, while most others have not.

Then the harder story. The American insurer UnitedHealthcare used a tool called nH Predict to judge claims for nursing-home and rehabilitation care after hospital stays. Families sued in late 2023, and the complaint alleged that the AI's predicted recovery times were used to deny ongoing care, even when treating doctors said the patient still needed it. The company denies the tool made coverage decisions by itself. The suit also said case managers were judged by how often they agreed with the tool, which is exactly the tell that decision support has become decision substitute: the staff using the tool are evaluated or graded on how closely they follow the AI's recommendation. A system labelled advisory on paper is binding in practice if agreement is what gets you a good review.

The deepest asymmetry is structural rather than technical. Investigations by STAT News and by ProPublica documented high denial rates with little human review across several insurers, and the shape of the problem is this: one model decides for thousands while each patient appeals alone, so the asymmetry favors the insurer. Which is why the practical advice to an affected family is procedural. Ask explicitly for a human-reviewed appeal, in writing, and keep the paperwork.

dark-patterns-gambling.context_blurb:
A dark pattern is an interface built to push you toward what makes the company money at your expense, and once you can name the moves you stop falling for most of them. AI did not invent any of this. It made every move personal.

Start with the catalogue. When signing up takes one glowing button and cancelling takes six menus and a phone call, those are dark patterns in user design, named by the designer Harry Brignull around 2010. One has a particularly ugly name: confirmshaming, where pressure language like "No thanks, I prefer overpaying" is presented as the opt-out, so declining feels like an embarrassing admission. When a company insists it lets users choose, look at the number of clicks to refuse versus to accept, because the asymmetry of friction is the real policy. Badges, points and login streaks are gamification to drive engagement, borrowed from game design to build a daily habit. That evening buzz about three new updates exists to pull you back to the app, not to inform you. And when a feed hides its clocks and timestamps, that is deliberate, because without time cues, users lose track of how long they've been scrolling.

The reward science underneath is old. B.F. Skinner's variable-ratio reinforcement schedules are the most addictive reward structure in his operant-conditioning research, and they power slot machines and a great many app interactions alike. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein's 2008 book called the gentler version a nudge, a design push that steers without forbidding. What AI adds is reach, because AI can personalize nudges to each user, making them more effective. In the hands of a manipulator it personalizes the manipulation, finding the exact wording or layout that works on you specifically, which split-testing on averages never could. The technology itself picks no side. A budgeting app and a betting app can run the same technique with opposite goals, where one serves your interest and the other serves the platform's.

Betting is where the cost is cash. Sports-betting apps study how and when their users bet in order to maximize how much users bet, then time the free-bet offers and push alerts accordingly. AI lets the platform individually identify which users gamble compulsively and which can be most efficiently induced to lose more money. That is the heart of the objection, since personalized inducements work especially well on the people most likely to be harmed by them. Even the giveaways are engineered: a deposit bonus usually comes with forced rollover, so the bonus only releases after additional wagers reach a multiple of the deposit, and accepting the free money compels more play.

Dating apps show the same logic without the villainy. They are optimized for keeping users on the app, because that is where the subscription revenue lives. And the conflict is structural rather than wicked: if you find a partner and leave, the app loses a user. If matching too well leads users to leave the app, the system can learn to keep you swiping without finding success, which gives the algorithm an incentive to keep good matches scarce enough that users stay subscribed, so the optimization is structurally biased toward continued engagement. Investors are shown engagement numbers, not marriages.

One question is left over, and it is political rather than technical. Defaults exist whether anyone intends them or not, so the thing to ask of a platform shaping choices for billions is who chose the defaults, and what accountability exists when those defaults harm users, given that the designers can't be voted out the way governments can.

smart-home-cameras.context_blurb: Smart-home cameras record continuously or on motion and typically store the footage in the manufacturer's cloud. Who else can see that footage is a longer list than most buyers expect: the manufacturer, law enforcement responding to a subpoena, in some cases law enforcement through partnership programs that bypassed warrant requirements. One major camera maker was found to have shared footage with police without warrants in multiple cases before changing its policy under public pressure. The AI side of these products — face recognition on familiar visitors, package detection, person-vs-animal distinction — is genuinely useful and also builds a per-household database of movement patterns stored on the manufacturer's servers. Recognizing this matters because 'my camera' is a different privacy object from 'camera footage sitting on a company's servers' — the first implies control that the second does not actually provide. Local-storage camera options exist and keep the footage physically at home, which is a meaningful privacy choice for households that want the security benefit without the data trail.

ai-copyright-artists.context_blurb:
Every generative model learned from something, and in the early 2020s the something was mostly scraped from the open web without asking. That single fact set off the sharpest legal fight of the AI era, and it is still unresolved, which matters to anyone planning a creative career.

Stability AI shipped its Stable Diffusion image model with downloadable weights in August 2022, trained on a vast web-scraped collection called LAION-5B that included work by living painters and illustrators who were never asked. Artists filed a class action in 2023; Getty Images sued separately. Years of litigation later, the uncomfortable pattern is about who gets a seat: the eventual rules favour whoever was at the table while the rules were settled, which means the laboratories and the large rights-holders, not the individual creators whose work was scraped.

Music followed the same path. Stable Audio, Udio and Suno will build a full-band song out of one sentence of instruction, and in June 2024 the recording industry sued the last two of those for training on copyrighted recordings. Whichever way the verdicts fall, they settle something narrower than people expect, because training data choices shape what kinds of art the resulting AI can, and can't, produce. What a model never saw, it cannot imitate; a dataset is a capability decision, an ethics decision and a bias decision at once.

hinton-radiology-prediction.context_blurb:
Addressing an audience of doctors in 2016, Geoffrey Hinton said the training of new radiologists ought to stop, because deep learning would replace them inside five years. It is the most quoted wrong prediction in the field, and worth knowing exactly how it went wrong.

Nearly a decade on, radiologists are still in demand, and American surveys report a shortage rather than a glut. Meanwhile the imaging tools did arrive and they do work, for lung nodules, diabetic eye damage, mammograms and some skin cancers. What they became was a second reader catching missed details, with the trained radiologist still making the final call. In mammography that workflow is now standard: the human reads the scan, the software flags regions, the human looks again, which makes the AI a second reader, a different perspective that may catch things the human missed. Trials in Sweden found more cancers caught without a flood of false alarms. Stated as the answer to Hinton's forecast, AI became a second-reader and triage tool, flagging suspicious findings for the radiologist to review, not replacing the human.

Why did a brilliant researcher miss by so much? Because a benchmark is not a workflow. Getting into a hospital requires regulatory clearance for a specific clinical use, integration with the imaging systems, insurance codes, patient trust, and above all a named human who is answerable when a diagnosis is missed. None of that appears in a test score. Carry the lesson forward to every confident claim about which profession falls next.
