ai-chips-arms-race.context_blurb:
Behind every chatbot demonstration stands a very physical supply chain of silicon, steel and megawatts. Training a frontier model takes specialised chips by the tens of thousands, the electricity to drive them, and buildings to hold both. Once you can see that layer, the policy fights make more sense, because most of them are arguments about who gets the hardware.

Start with the chokepoint. TSMC, based in Taiwan, fabricates the bulk of frontier AI silicon, and a Chinese blockade or invasion of Taiwan would freeze the global supply of leading-edge chips overnight. Nvidia draws the designs for the H100 and the accelerators that followed, but owns no factory; roughly nine in ten of the world's most advanced logic chips are printed on that one island. America's CHIPS Act of 2022 and the new fabrication plants rising in Arizona are both answers to that single fact, and so is the Pentagon's interest in the Taiwan Strait.

Washington's other answer was a blockade of its own. From October 2022, tightened repeatedly in the years after, the United States barred the sale of its best AI chips to China. The security reasoning is real, and so is a side effect that gets less airtime: export-control regimes concentrate AI power in fewer trusted actors, so the world's frontier compute increasingly runs in a small number of allied data centers. The rules also proved leaky. Then the Chinese laboratory DeepSeek published models with downloadable weights late in 2024 that scored near the American frontier, trained with fewer of the top chips and at a far lower reported cost. The lesson was that capable AI can be developed without the latest US-made chips, so chip controls cannot fully prevent capable models from reaching the world.

Then follow the money, because the bills have grown sovereign-sized. Sam Altman went hunting for capital in the Gulf in early 2024, in Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, with a figure reported as high as seven trillion dollars for new chip plants, more than the yearly output of any national economy but America's and China's. Instead of Silicon Valley he asked sovereign wealth funds, and that choice is the tell: compute, meaning chips, electricity, and the data centers to house them, is the real bottleneck for frontier AI, and the amounts of capital required have grown beyond what private US venture funds can supply alone. Within a year the Emirati fund MGX stood among the founding partners of the Stargate compute project announced in January 2025, and Saudi and Singaporean money had bought into American laboratories. Foreign government capital is now embedded in major US AI firms, which does not automatically compromise these companies, but it creates real dependencies and influence relationships worth watching.

ai-slop-and-publishing.context_blurb:
AI slop is the nickname for mass-produced machine text now filling parts of the open web: articles that read smoothly and say nothing, product blurbs that sound like reviews but mention no particular product, posts written for a feed rather than a reader. The economics explain it. Plausible prose costs almost nothing to make, and the systems that promote content do not reward quality in any specific way.

The reading habit is calibration rather than refusal. When a piece feels strangely smooth and balanced, with no strong claim, no anecdote, no risky opinion and no author's voice, suspect a machine, because AI-generated text is now common in marketing, news summaries, and customer-service content, and knowing the tells lets you weight it appropriately. A generated product description that is merely present costs you nothing. A generated opinion column pretending to be experience costs you your judgment.

Profiles are the harder case, because by the middle of the decade a few cheap tools could assemble a whole invented person: a face that belongs to nobody, a credible biography, a year of filler posts. Such accounts spread across dating apps, social networks and professional sites, running romance frauds, pushing propaganda or farming attention for money. Detector tools are unreliable in both directions, so the defence is procedural. Assume any single signal can be faked, and verify through independent channels, including video calls, mutual contacts and real-world meetings, before trust escalates.

andrej-karpathy.context_blurb:
Andrej Karpathy is the rare figure who has built frontier AI and then spent his time explaining it to everybody else. Slovak-born, he took a doctorate in computer vision at Stanford under Fei-Fei Li, and then walked a career path that doubles as a map of the industry.

He started at OpenAI, as a founding member when the lab was launched in 2015. Two years later he left for a job steering physical machines rather than conversations: Tesla Autopilot, the team building Tesla's self-driving car software. The whole arc runs OpenAI as a founding member, then Tesla where he led Autopilot, then back to OpenAI before going independent in 2024.

The second half of his reputation is the part that reaches ordinary learners. His tutorials and code walkthroughs have taught a generation of developers what's actually inside a neural network, building one from nothing, line by line, in Python, then a tokenizer, then a small GPT. The series are free on YouTube, and hundreds of thousands of people have followed along.

Why does a video series matter to a subject this large? Because he makes the internals of LLMs concrete and learnable, so anyone willing to spend the time can follow along and understand what's happening inside the systems people use. And because of who is doing the teaching: quality educational content from a founding insider directly counters the mystification of AI and helps more people understand how the technology actually works. Public argument about AI is shaped partly by who feels entitled to join it. Mystification narrows that circle; a clear explanation with the maths showing widens it.

browser-extensions.context_blurb:
An extension is a small add-on program that slots into Chrome, Firefox or Edge and gives the browser a new trick: blocking advertisements, checking grammar, and lately summarising a page or drafting a reply with AI. They install in two clicks and are then forgotten, which is the problem, because to do their work they ask for permission and almost nobody reads the request.

Read it. The one that matters says the add-on may read and change your data on every site you visit, and the extension can read every page you visit and may send the content to a remote AI server. That is not an abstract risk. The permission lets the extension see every page you visit, including banking, email, and private chats, and send the content anywhere its owner likes. An AI add-on genuinely needs some of this to summarise what is on your screen; the content has to travel somewhere to be processed.

So the question is who is on the other end, and how he gets paid. Free = your data is likely the product, so read the privacy policy and permissions carefully before installing anything with that reach. The sharper version, worth asking out loud: how is the company making money, and when the honest reply is that it sells user data, the price is too high. Freemium is fine, advertising is a warning, and brokerage is a no. A short cheerful privacy policy with a line about sharing aggregated data with partners usually means your browsing history is for sale.

One more habit, because an add-on you trusted in 2023 is not necessarily the same software today. Developers sell their extensions and accounts get breached, and the new owner pushes an update to everyone who already installed it; that is how a coupon finder becomes a password thief overnight. So periodically audit installed extensions and remove ones you don't actively use, since long-tail extensions are a known supply-chain risk. Open your browser's extensions page every few months and delete anything you have not touched in two. For the few you keep, prefer a paid tool or an open-source one from a developer with a reputation to lose.

predictive-policing.context_blurb: Predictive policing is the use of software to forecast where crime is likely to happen, or who is likely to be involved, so that a police department can decide where to send officers. In the 2010s departments in several large US cities bought such tools from private vendors; the best-known product divided a city map into small squares and highlighted some of them for each shift. The pitch was attractive: use data instead of hunches, and put limited patrols where they will do the most good. Independent researchers and community groups later examined how these systems were trained and what they did over time, and several cities ended their contracts. The topic matters because the question at its heart — what was the model trained on, and who checks its results? — applies to many other AI tools that governments use to make decisions about people.

fraud-detection-and-finance.context_blurb:
Banks were doing machine learning while the rest of us were still arguing about dial-up. Card fraud detection has run on learned models since the 1990s, which makes it a fine example of old AI that quietly works, noticed only on the day it saves you or embarrasses you at a petrol station.

The mechanism is unglamorous and worth knowing. The system models your normal spending patterns and flags transactions far outside them. When your phone buzzes about a blocked charge in Berlin ten minutes after lunch in Chicago, it has been checking your spending patterns against the record of how you usually buy. What it hunts for is simply patterns that don't match yours. So the trigger is unusual location or behaviour compared to your normal spending, which is why a holiday three thousand miles from home can freeze a card over a two-dollar snack. Statisticians call this anomaly detection, and the same shape runs your spam filter and your employer's network alarms.

The other side of finance is faster and less reassuring. The firms that trade by algorithm at high frequency place their servers beside the exchange to shave microseconds off an order, and together they handle a large slice of American trading volume. On 6 May 2010 those systems met each other with nobody in between, producing the Flash Crash, when the Dow dropped roughly a thousand points in minutes and recovered the same day, driven by algorithmic feedback loops. Later rules added some circuit breakers without changing the basic dynamic. Markets are infrastructure, and this part of the infrastructure now runs faster than any human can supervise in real time.

ai-and-jobs.context_blurb:
Every wave of automation arrives with a list of doomed professions. By the middle of the 2020s there was evidence instead of prophecy: businesses had put generative AI to work at scale in stock photography and in telephone support, and the sales figures and satisfaction surveys were in. The lesson is that a job is a bundle of tasks, and the machine took some of them.

Stock photography lost its middle. Adobe, Shutterstock and Getty watched sales of generic, royalty-free pictures slide through 2023 and 2024, because a blog header or a product mockup no longer needs a camera. What the forecasters got wrong was the rest of the trade: high-end editorial, journalism, wedding, and brand photography stayed strong, because original real-world capture is still where humans are needed. Somebody has to stand at the event, direct a nervous couple, and light this particular bottle in this particular room.

Telephone and chat support tells the same story in another key. Klarna said in 2024 that its assistant was doing the work of roughly seven hundred agents, Lyft and others made similar announcements, and independent surveys found callers rated the machines below the people they replaced. The honest summary is double-edged: AI handles routine, well-scoped questions cheaply at scale, but customer satisfaction often drops, and human agents are still needed for the harder cases. Banks, airlines and large retailers that made the switch work all followed one rule. The machines handled known, scripted requests (balance check, password reset, order status) well; they handled emotional, ambiguous, or escalating complaints poorly, so the firms that built a fast escape hatch to a person kept their customers and the firms that hid it lost them.
